verses.134:17: they have ears, yet they do not listen; indeed, there is no breath at all in their mouths.
verses.134:18: Their makers will become like them, everyone who trusts in them.
verses.134:19: House of Israel, bless the LORD; house of Aaron, bless the LORD;
verses.134:20: house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD.
verses.134:21: Blessed be the LORD from Zion, the One dwelling in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!
verses.135:1: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good, for His loyal love lasts forever.
verses.135:2: Give thanks to the God of gods, for His loyal love lasts forever.
verses.135:3: Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:4: to the One who alone performs great wonders, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:5: to the One who made the heavens with understanding, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:6: to the One who spread out the earth over the waters, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:7: to the One who made great lights, for His loyal love lasts forever:
verses.135:8: the sun for dominion over the day, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:9: the moon and stars for dominion over the night, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:10: to the One who struck down Egypt in their firstborn, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:11: and brought out Israel from their midst, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:12: with a strong hand and with an outstretched arm, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:13: to the One who split the Sea of Reeds into parts, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:14: and caused Israel to pass through its midst, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:15: yet overturned Pharaoh and his army in the Sea of Reeds, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:16: to the One who led His people in the wilderness, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:17: to the One who struck down great kings, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:18: and killed mighty kings, for His loyal love lasts forever:
verses.135:19: Sihon king of the Amorites, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:20: and Og king of Bashan, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:21: and gave their land as an inheritance, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:22: an inheritance for Israel, His servant, for His loyal love lasts forever.
verses.135:23: He is the One who remembered us in our low condition, for His loyal love lasts forever,
verses.135:24: and delivered us from our adversaries, for His loyal love lasts forever;
verses.135:25: He gives food to all flesh, for His loyal love lasts forever.
verses.135:26: Give thanks to the God of the heavens, for His loyal love lasts forever.
verses.136:1: Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and also wept as we remembered Zion.
verses.136:2: On the poplars in her midst, we hung our lyres.
verses.136:3: For there our captors asked us for words of song, and our tormentors for joy: "Sing for us from the songs of Zion!"
verses.136:4: How can we sing the song of the LORD on foreign soil?
verses.136:5: If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget.
verses.136:6: May my tongue cling to my palate if I do not remember you, if I do not lift Jerusalem above the peak of my joy.
verses.136:7: Remember, LORD, against the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, those who said, "Strip her bare, strip her bare, down to her foundation!"
verses.136:8: Daughter of Babylon, the devastated one, happy is the one who pays you back the treatment you dealt to us.
verses.136:9: Happy is the one who seizes and smashes your infants against the rock.
verses.137:1: Of David. I will give thanks to You with my whole heart; in the presence of the gods I will sing praise to You.
verses.137:2: I will bow down toward Your holy temple and give thanks to Your name because of Your loyal love and Your truth, for You have made Your word great above all Your name.
verses.137:3: In the day I called out, You answered me; You emboldened me in my soul with strength.
verses.137:4: LORD, all the kings of the earth will give thanks to You, because they have heard the words of Your mouth.
verses.137:5: And they will sing of the LORD's ways, because the glory of the LORD is great.
verses.137:6: For the LORD is high, yet He looks on the lowly, and He knows the haughty from a distance.
verses.137:7: Though I walk in the midst of distress, You will keep me alive; against the anger of my enemies You will stretch out Your hand, and Your right hand will save me.
verses.137:8: The LORD will bring it to completion on my behalf; LORD, Your loyal love endures forever; do not abandon the works of Your hands.
verses.138:1: For the music director. Of David. A psalm. LORD, You have examined me, and You know me.
verses.138:2: You know my sitting down and my rising up; You perceive my thought from a distance.
verses.138:3: You sift my path and my lying down, and You are familiar with all my ways.
verses.138:4: For there is not a word on my tongue; see, LORD, You know all of it.
verses.138:5: Behind and in front You have hemmed me in, and You have set Your hand upon me.
verses.138:6: Such knowledge is too marvelous for me; it is set high; I cannot reach it.
verses.138:7: Where could I go from Your Spirit? And where from Your presence could I flee?
verses.138:8: If I ascend to the heavens, there You are; and if I spread my bed in Sheol, look, You are there.
verses.138:9: If I lift up the wings of the dawn, if I settle at the farthest end of the sea,
verses.138:10: even there Your hand will guide me, and Your right hand will grasp me.
verses.138:11: And if I say, "Surely darkness will engulf me, and the light around me will be night,"
verses.138:12: even darkness is not dark before You, and night shines like the day; as darkness is, so is light.
verses.138:13: For You created my innermost parts; You wove me together in the womb of my mother.
verses.138:14: I will give thanks to You because I am awesomely and marvelously formed; Your works are marvelous, and my soul knows it thoroughly.
verses.138:15: My bones were not hidden from You when I was fashioned in secret, embroidered in the lowest parts of the earth.
verses.138:16: Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in Your book all of them were written; days were formed, and to Him belongs one among them.
verses.138:17: And to me, how precious are Your thoughts, God! How immense are their totals!
verses.138:18: Were I to count them, they would be more numerous than the sand; I awaken, and still I am with You.
verses.138:19: If only You would kill the wicked, God! And men of bloodshed, turn away from me!
verses.138:20: For they speak of You with malicious intent; Your adversaries take up Your name in vain.
verses.138:21: LORD, do I not hate those who hate You, and detest those who rise against You?
verses.138:22: With utter hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me.
verses.138:23: Examine me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my troubled thoughts;
verses.138:24: and see if there is any way of pain in me, and guide me in the eternal way.
verses.139:1: For the music director. A psalm of David.
verses.139:2: Rescue me, LORD, from the evil man; guard me from the man of violence,
verses.139:3: those who plot evils in their heart; every day they stir up wars.
verses.139:4: They have sharpened their tongue like a snake; a viper's venom is beneath their lips. Selah.
verses.139:5: Keep me, LORD, from the hands of the wicked; guard me from the man of violence, those who plot to overthrow my steps.
verses.139:6: The arrogant have concealed a trap and cords for me; they have spread out a net alongside the path; they have set snares for me. Selah.
verses.139:7: I said to the LORD, "You are my God." Listen attentively, LORD, to the voice of my pleas for grace.
verses.139:8: GOD, the Lord, strength of my salvation, You have shielded my head on the day of warfare.
verses.139:9: LORD, do not grant the desires of the wicked; do not advance his scheme, or else they will become exalted. Selah.
verses.139:10: The head of those who encircle me—may the trouble of their lips cover them.
verses.139:11: May glowing coals fall upon them; may He cast them into the fire, into deep pits, so that they do not rise.
verses.139:12: A slanderous man will not be established in the land; as for the man of violence, evil will hunt him down to headlong ruin.
verses.139:13: I know that the LORD will uphold the cause of the afflicted, the justice of the needy.
verses.139:14: Indeed, the righteous will give thanks to Your name; the upright will live in Your presence.
verses.140:1: A psalm of David. LORD, I have called to You; hurry to me. Listen closely to my voice when I call to You.
verses.140:2: May my prayer be established as incense before You, the raising of my hands as an evening offering.
verses.140:3: Place a guard at my mouth, LORD; watch over the door of my lips.
verses.140:4: Do not turn my heart to an evil matter, to engage in deeds in wickedness with men who are workers of iniquity, and may I not dine on their delicacies.
verses.140:5: May a righteous man strike me in loyal love and rebuke me; it is oil for the head—may my head not refuse it. For even still, my prayer is against their evil deeds.
verses.140:6: Their judges will be cast down along the sides of the crag, and they will hear my words, for they are sweet.
verses.140:7: As one plows and splits open the ground, our bones have been dispersed at the mouth of Sheol.
verses.140:8: For toward You are my eyes, GOD, the Lord; in You I have taken refuge; do not pour out my soul.
verses.140:9: Guard me from the grasp of the trap they have set for me, and from the snares of workers of iniquity.
verses.140:10: May the wicked fall into their own nets, while at the same time I myself pass through.
verses.141:1: A Maskil of David, while he was in the cave; a prayer.
verses.141:2: I cry out with my voice to the LORD; with my voice I plead to the LORD for favor.
verses.141:3: Before Him I pour out my complaint; before Him I declare my distress.
verses.141:4: When my spirit grows faint within me, You Yourself know my path. Along the road where I walk, they have concealed a trap for me.
verses.141:5: Look toward the right and see: there is no one who acknowledges me; escape has vanished from me; there is no one caring for my soul.
verses.141:6: I have cried out to You, LORD; I said, "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living."
verses.141:7: Pay attention to my outcry, for I have been reduced very low; rescue me from my pursuers, for they are stronger than I.
verses.141:8: Bring my soul out of confinement to give thanks to Your name; the righteous will encircle me, because You will deal generously with me.
verses.142:1: A psalm of David. LORD, hear my prayer; listen closely to my pleas for favor. By Your faithfulness answer me, by Your righteousness.
verses.142:2: And do not come into judgment with Your servant, for no living being will be righteous before You.
verses.142:3: For an enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the earth; he has caused me to dwell in dark places, like the dead of long ago.
verses.142:4: So my spirit has grown faint within me; inside me my heart is desolate.
verses.142:5: I remember days from ancient times; I meditate on all Your deeds; I reflect on the work of Your hands.
verses.142:6: I spread out my hands toward You; my soul is like a parched land for You. Selah.
verses.142:7: Hurry, answer me, LORD; my spirit is spent. Do not hide Your face from me, or else I will be like those who descend into the pit.
verses.142:8: Let me hear Your loyal love in the morning, for in You I have trusted. Make known to me the way I should walk, for to You I have lifted up my soul.
verses.142:9: Rescue me from my enemies, LORD; with You I have hidden myself.
verses.142:10: Instruct me to do Your will, for You are my God; may Your good Spirit guide me in a level land.
verses.142:11: For the sake of Your name, LORD, keep me alive; in Your righteousness, bring my soul out of distress.
verses.142:12: And in Your loyal love, wipe out my enemies, and destroy all the foes of my soul, for I am Your servant.
verses.143:1: Of David. Blessed be the LORD, my rock, who trains my hands for combat, my fingers for war.
verses.143:2: He is my loyal love and my fortress, my high refuge and my own rescuer, my shield, and in Him I take refuge, the One who subdues my people beneath me.
verses.143:3: LORD, what is a human being, that You know him, a son of mortal man, that You consider him?
verses.143:4: A human being resembles a breath; his days are like a shadow passing by.
verses.143:5: LORD, bend down Your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and let them smoke.
verses.143:6: Flash lightning and scatter them; send Your arrows and throw them into confusion.
verses.143:7: Reach out Your hands from on high; free me and deliver me from many waters, from the hand of foreigners,
verses.143:8: whose mouths speak untruth, and whose right hand is a right hand of deception.
verses.143:9: God, I will sing a new song to You; with a harp of ten strings I will make music to You,
verses.143:10: the One who gives salvation to kings, who frees David His servant from an evil sword.
verses.143:11: Free me and deliver me from the hand of foreigners, whose mouths speak untruth, and whose right hand is a right hand of deception,
verses.143:12: so that our sons may be like saplings grown large in their youth, our daughters like corner pillars carved in the design of a palace;
verses.143:13: our storehouses full, bringing forth one kind after another; our flocks producing thousands, even tens of thousands in our open fields;
verses.143:14: our cattle heavily laden; no breach and no going out, and no outcry in our open squares.
verses.143:15: Happy is the people for whom it is like this; happy is the people whose God is the LORD.
verses.144:1: A praise of David. I will exalt You, my God, the King, and I will bless Your name forever and ever.
verses.144:2: Each day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever.
verses.144:3: Great is the LORD and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no searching out His greatness.
verses.144:4: Generation to generation will extol Your works, and they will proclaim Your mighty deeds.
verses.144:5: I will meditate on the splendor of the glory of Your majesty and on the accounts of Your wonders.
verses.144:6: And they will tell of the power of Your awe-inspiring acts, and I will recount Your greatness.
verses.144:7: They will pour out the remembrance of Your abundant goodness, and they will sing joyfully of Your righteousness.
verses.144:8: Gracious and compassionate is the LORD, slow to anger and great in loyal love.
verses.144:9: Good is the LORD to all, and His compassion is over all His works.
verses.144:10: All Your works will thank You, LORD, and Your faithful ones will bless You.
verses.144:11: They will tell of Your kingdom's glory and speak of Your mighty power,
verses.144:12: to make known to the children of mankind His mighty deeds and the glory of the splendor of His kingdom.
verses.144:13: Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and Your dominion extends through every generation.
verses.144:14: The LORD supports all who are falling and lifts upright all who are bent down.
verses.144:15: The eyes of all look expectantly to You, and You give them their food in its time,
verses.144:16: opening Your hand and satisfying every living creature's desire.
verses.144:17: Righteous is the LORD in all His ways, and faithful in all His works.
verses.144:18: Near is the LORD to all who call to Him, to all who call to Him in truth.
verses.144:19: He will fulfill the desire of those who fear Him, and will hear their cry for help and save them.
verses.144:20: The LORD guards all who love Him, but all the wicked He will wipe out.
verses.144:21: The praise of the LORD my mouth will speak, and may all flesh bless His holy name forever and ever.
verses.145:1: Praise the LORD! My soul, praise the LORD!
verses.145:2: I will praise the LORD throughout my life; I will make music to my God as long as I exist.
verses.145:3: Do not trust in nobles, in a human being, with whom there is no salvation.
verses.145:4: His breath goes out, he returns to his ground; on that day his plans perish.
verses.145:5: Happy is the one who has the God of Jacob as his help, whose hope is upon the LORD his God,
verses.145:6: the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea and everything that is in them, who keeps truth forever,
verses.145:7: who carries out justice for the oppressed, who gives bread to the hungry. The LORD releases those who are bound.
verses.145:8: The LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the LORD lifts upright those who are bent down; the LORD loves the righteous.
verses.145:9: The LORD guards the resident foreigners; He sustains the orphan and the widow, but the way of the wicked He subverts.
verses.145:10: The LORD will reign forever, your God, Zion, from generation to generation. Praise the LORD!
verses.146:1: Praise the LORD! For it is good to make music to our God, for it is pleasant; praise is fitting.
verses.146:2: The LORD builds Jerusalem; He gathers the banished of Israel.
verses.146:3: He is the One who heals those broken in heart and bandages their wounds.
verses.146:4: He reckons the number of the stars; He calls them all by name.
verses.146:5: Our Lord is great and vast in strength; His understanding is without number.
verses.146:6: The LORD upholds the humble; He brings the wicked low to the ground.
verses.146:7: Respond to the LORD with thanksgiving; make music to our God with the lyre,
verses.146:8: who covers the skies with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who causes grass to sprout on the mountains.
verses.146:9: He gives to the animals their food, to the raven's young that call out.
verses.146:10: He does not delight in the might of the horse; He is not pleased with the legs of a man.
verses.146:11: The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him, with those who wait for His loyal love.
verses.147:1: Laud the LORD, Jerusalem! Praise your God, Zion!
verses.147:2: For He has reinforced the bars of your gates; He has blessed your children in your midst.
verses.147:3: He sets your territory at peace; He satisfies you with the choicest wheat.
verses.147:4: He sends His utterance to the earth; swiftly His word runs.
verses.147:5: He bestows snow like wool; He strews frost like ash.
verses.147:6: He hurls His ice like morsels; before His cold, who can stand?
verses.147:7: He sends His word and makes them melt. He makes His wind blow; waters flow.
verses.147:8: He proclaims His words to Jacob, His decrees and His rulings to Israel.
verses.147:9: He has not done so for any nation; and as for rulings, they do not know them. Praise the LORD!
verses.148:1: Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the heights.
verses.148:2: Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His armies.
verses.148:3: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all bright stars.
verses.148:4: Praise Him, heavens of the heavens, and the waters above the heavens.
verses.148:5: May they praise the name of the LORD, for He Himself commanded, and they were created.
verses.148:6: And He stationed them forever and ever; He set a decree, and it will not pass away.
verses.148:7: Praise the LORD from the earth, sea monsters and all depths,
verses.148:8: fire and hail, snow and fog, storm wind carrying out His word,
verses.148:9: mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars,
verses.148:10: wild animals and all livestock, crawling creatures and winged birds,
verses.148:11: kings of the earth and all nations, rulers and all judges of the earth,
verses.148:12: young men and young women as well, the elderly together with children.
verses.148:13: May they praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is lifted high; His splendor is above earth and heaven.
verses.148:14: And He has raised a horn for His people, praise for all His loyal ones, for the children of Israel, a people close to Him. Praise the LORD!
verses.149:1: Praise the LORD! Sing a new song to the LORD, His praise in the assembly of the devoted ones.
verses.149:2: May Israel be joyful in its Maker; may the sons of Zion exult in their King.
verses.149:3: May they praise His name with dancing; with hand drum and lyre may they make music to Him.
verses.149:4: For the LORD is pleased with His people; He adorns the humble with deliverance.
verses.149:5: May the devoted ones rejoice in glory; may they shout with joy on their beds.
verses.149:6: High praises of God are in their throats, and double-edged swords are in their hands,
verses.149:7: to carry out vengeance on the nations, punishments on the peoples,
verses.149:8: to bind their kings in chains and their nobles in iron fetters,
verses.149:9: to carry out on them the written judgment. It is an honor for all His devoted ones. Praise the LORD!
verses.150:1: Praise the LORD! Praise God in His holy place; praise Him in the expanse of His strength.
verses.150:2: Praise Him for His deeds of might; praise Him according to the abundance of His greatness.
verses.150:3: Praise Him with the blast of the ram's horn; praise Him with lute and lyre.
verses.150:4: Praise Him with hand drum and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute.
verses.150:5: Praise Him with resonant cymbals; praise Him with clashing cymbals.
verses.150:6: May all that has breath praise the LORD! Praise the LORD!

notes.1:2: Hebrew torah literally means "instruction" or "teaching." The Qal verb rendered "meditates" denotes murmuring or reciting softly in reflection, and the same root recurs in 2:1 for the peoples plotting emptiness.
notes.1:3: The noun rendered "channels" (palge) refers specifically to divided watercourses or irrigation canals. The final verb is Hiphil imperfect, functioning either internally ("everything he does will succeed") or causatively ("he brings everything he does to success").
notes.1:5: In this legal setting ("in the judgment"), the Qal verb "stand up" means to withstand scrutiny or remain acquitted rather than mere physical posture.
notes.2:1: The Qal verb rendered "are in tumult" occurs only here in Biblical Hebrew, denoting restless commotion or thronging. "Plot" uses the same verbal root (hagah) translated "meditates" in 1:2, here taking the noun "emptiness" as its direct object.
notes.2:7: Following the Masoretic accentuation, the pause falls after "decree" (preceded by the preposition el, "concerning"), making "the LORD" the subject of "said"; some instead construe "the decree of the LORD: He said to me." "Have fathered you" translates the Qal perfect of yalad, here expressing royal adoption at enthronement.
notes.2:9: The Masoretic vocalization reads this Qal verb from the root ra'a ("break, smash"), matching the parallel Piel verb "shatter"; the Septuagint instead read the same consonants from the root "shepherd/rule."
notes.2:12: The phrase "Kiss the son" uses the Piel imperative of "kiss" (a gesture of royal homage) with bar, widely taken as the poetic or Aramaic word for "son" (cf. Proverbs 31:2, echoing 2:7), though some understand it from Hebrew bar ("purely" or "in purity"). "Along the path" renders an adverbial accusative echoing 1:6.
notes.3:1: Following the Masoretic Hebrew versification, the psalm superscription is numbered as verse 1, so the body of the psalm begins at verse 2.
notes.3:3: Hebrew yeshu'atah is a poetic lengthened form of "deliverance" (yeshu'ah), the same noun that recurs in 3:9. "Selah" (here and in 3:5, 3:9) is a transliterated liturgical or musical term of uncertain meaning.
notes.3:8: The Hiphil perfect "have struck" and Piel perfect "have shattered" follow the opening imperatives to ground the appeal either in God's past acts of rescue or in confident assurance of deliverance.
notes.4:4: The verb hiflah (Hiphil of palah) means to set apart or distinguish, highlighting God's special regard for the chasid (faithful one, one bound in covenant loyalty).
notes.4:5: Rigzu (Qal imperative of ragaz) primarily means tremble or be agitated (rendered be angry in the Septuagint); speak in your heart is a Hebrew idiom for silent inward reflection.
notes.4:7: Nesah is an unusual Qal imperative form of nasa (lift up), spelled with samekh instead of sin and echoing the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25-26.
notes.4:9: Levadad (alone) is linked by the Masoretic atnah accent with You, LORD, though syntactically it may also modify the psalmist's dwelling (cause me to dwell alone in security).
notes.5:1: Ha-nechilot (the Nehiloth) is a unique musical heading of uncertain etymology, traditionally associated with flutes or wind instruments.
notes.5:4: Eerokh (Qal imperfect of arakh, arrange or set in order) has no explicit object in Hebrew and may denote either ordering one's verbal plea or laying out a morning sacrifice.
notes.5:9: Ketiv/Qere: ketiv reads hwshr (treating the root yashar as an initial-waw verb in the Hiphil imperative), while qere reads hayshar (preserving the initial yod); both mean make level or straight.
notes.5:10: MT has a singular suffix in befihu (in his mouth), a distributive singular referring to each foe before shifting to plural suffixes; yachaliqun (Hiphil of chalaq, make smooth) is an idiom for flattering speech.
notes.5:13: Taaterennu is Qal imperfect of atar (surround or encircle, whereas the Piel stem means crown); tsinnah denotes a large full-body shield rather than a smaller buckler.
notes.6:1: Ha-sheminit (the Sheminith, literally the eighth) is a musical term understood either as an eight-stringed instrument or as a lower octave or mode.
notes.6:4: Ketiv/Qere: ketiv writes the shorter defective spelling wt of the second-person masculine singular pronoun, while qere supplies the standard spelling we-attah (and You).
notes.6:7: Both ascheh (Hiphil of sachah, cause to swim) and amseh (Hiphil of masah, melt or dissolve) are vivid poetic hyperboles depicting profuse weeping.
notes.6:11: Yibbahalu (Niphal of bahal, be terrified) echoes the psalmist's own affliction in 6:3-4 (nivhalu, nivhalah), marking a dramatic reversal upon his enemies.
notes.7:1: Shiggaion (Hebrew shiggayon) is a musical or poetic term of uncertain meaning, occurring elsewhere in the plural in Habakkuk 3:1.
notes.7:5: The verb form (Piel of chalats) regularly means "deliver" or "rescue" elsewhere in the Psalms, yielding a contrastive aside here; some lexicons posit a distinct sense "strip" or "plunder" to run parallel with the preceding clause.
notes.7:6: The form yiraddof displays an unusual Masoretic pointing combining features of the Qal (yirdof) and Piel (yeraddef) stems of radaf ("pursue").
notes.7:10: Hebrew kelayot ("kidneys") is the idiomatic term for the seat of one's deepest emotions, desires, and inward motives.
notes.8:1: The Gittith (Hebrew ha-gittit) is a musical term of uncertain meaning, likely referring to a tune or instrument associated with Gath or winepresses.
notes.8:2: The Masoretic form tenah is anomalously pointed like the Qal imperative of natan ("give, set") after the relative pronoun asher; traditional Hebrew grammar construes it as a rare infinitive construct form with the sense "You who have set."
notes.8:6: Hebrew elohim ("God") can also denote "divine beings" or "heavenly beings," and ancient versions such as the Septuagint rendered it "angels."
notes.9:13: Following the Masoretic Qere anawim ("the humble"); the Ketiv reads aniyyim ("the afflicted").
notes.9:19: Following the Masoretic Qere aniyyim ("the afflicted"); the Ketiv reads anawim ("the humble").
notes.9:21: Hebrew morah is an orthographic variant of mora ("dread, terror"), with final he written in place of aleph.
notes.9:24: Following the Masoretic accents, berekh (Piel of barakh, "bless") takes the greedy person as its object; alternatively, the greedy person is the subject and berekh is used euphemistically for "curse," yielding "and the greedy one curses and spurns the LORD."
notes.9:31: Following two Masoretic Qere readings: yidkeh (Qal imperfect of dakah, "crouch, be crushed"; Ketiv we-dakhah) and two words chel ka'im ("company of the downcast," agreeing with the singular verb nafal; Ketiv chelka'im, "the helpless").
notes.9:33: Following the Masoretic Qere anawim ("the humble"); the Ketiv reads aniyyim ("the afflicted").
notes.10:1: The written ketiv reads a 2nd-person masculine plural Qal imperative matching the plural suffix of "your mountain," whereas the read qere (translated here) is a 2nd-person feminine singular imperative agreeing with feminine "my soul" and "bird." The Masoretic Hebrew lacks a preposition "like" before "bird," permitting a direct vocative rendering.
notes.10:3: Hebrew hashatot ("foundations" or "pillars") is a rare noun occurring only here and in Isaiah 19:10. The Qal perfect verb pa'al literally asks "what has a righteous one accomplished?" and functions rhetorically to express helplessness.
notes.10:6: The Masoretic Text reads pachim, plural of pach ("trap" or "snare"), echoing the bird imagery of 10:1. Because "fire and sulfur" follow, some interpreters instead associate the word with glowing coals.
notes.10:7: The noun paneimo ("His face") uses the poetic suffix -mo as a 3rd-person singular pronoun, with the 3rd-person plural verb yechezu taking singular "upright" collectively. Because "face" (panim) is grammatically plural in Hebrew, the clause can alternatively be read "His face gazes upon the upright."
notes.11:1: Hebrew hasheminit literally means "the eighth" (cf. 1 Chronicles 15:21), probably denoting either an eight-stringed instrument or a lower-octave musical mode.
notes.11:6: The terse clause ashit beyesha yafiach lo uses the Hiphil imperfect of puach ("breathe, pant, puff") in an unmarked relative clause, understood here as "in the deliverance for which he longs." Alternatively, taking puach as "scoff" or "snort," it may be rendered "I will set in safety the one at whom they scoff."
notes.11:7: Hebrew ba'alil la'aretz contains the unique noun alil, traditionally understood as a crucible or smelting furnace, with la'aretz denoting either a furnace set on the ground or an earthen vessel.
notes.11:8: The verb titzrennu carries the standard 3rd-person masculine singular energic suffix -ennu ("him"), shifting from plural "them" to each individual afflicted person as in 11:6, though some construe the suffix as 1st-person plural ("us").
notes.11:9: Hebrew zullut ("depravity" or "vileness") is a hapax legomenon derived from the root zalal ("be worthless, vile"), paired here with the Qal infinitive construct of rum ("rise high").
notes.12:2: The juxtaposition of ad-anah ("how long") with netzach ("forever" or "perpetually") creates a deliberate lament paradox expressing feelings of endless abandonment.
notes.12:3: Hebrew ashit etzot benafshi ("set counsels in my soul") depicts anxious inward deliberation. The adverb yomam means "by day" or "daily," with no mention of night in the Masoretic Text.
notes.12:5: Hebrew yecholtiv combines the 1st-person Qal perfect of yachol ("be able, prevail") directly with a 3rd-person singular object suffix, an idiom meaning "I have overpowered him."
notes.12:6: The verb yagel is a shortened Qal jussive form of gil ("exult"), paired with the 1st-person cohortative ashirah ("I will sing"), while gamal alai idiomatically denotes dealing generously or graciously with someone.
notes.13:3: The verb "become tainted" translates the Niphal perfect of Hebrew alach (to turn sour, spoil, or become morally tainted), distinguishing it from the Hiphil of shachat ("acted corruptly") in 13:1.
notes.13:4: Hebrew ammi ("my people") is understood here as David speaking of Israel, matching the third-person reference to the LORD in the same verse, though some interpreters take it as an unintroduced divine utterance ("My people").
notes.13:6: The Hiphil imperfect of bosh ("bring to shame") is translated conatively ("would bring ... to shame"), with Hebrew ki rendered adversatively ("yet"); some take ki causally, meaning the wicked mock the afflicted precisely because the LORD is his refuge.
notes.13:7: The idiom shuv shevut ("restore fortunes") derives most likely from the root shuv ("turn back, restore"), though traditionally it has also been linked to shavah ("take captive") and rendered "brings back the captivity of His people."
notes.14:1: The verb "sojourn" translates the Qal imperfect of gur (to stay temporarily as a guest under a host's protection), paired with the Qal imperfect of shakan ("dwell") in the parallel clause.
notes.14:3: The verb "spread slander" translates the Qal perfect of ragal (denominative from regel, "foot," literally going about talebearing), which occurs in the Qal stem only here in Biblical Hebrew.
notes.14:4: Following the Masoretic punctuation, the Niphal participle nivzeh ("a contemptible person") is read as the subject and the Niphal participle nimas ("is rejected") as the predicate; the two may also be construed the other way ("a rejected person is despised in his eyes"). Also, le-hara (Hiphil infinitive construct of ra'a) means "to his own detriment/hurt," whereas the Septuagint read "to his neighbor."
notes.15:2: The Masoretic Text vocalizes amart as a second-person feminine singular Qal perfect ("you have said"), traditionally explained as the psalmist addressing his soul; the consonants can also be read as a defective spelling of first-person singular amarti ("I have said"), as the Septuagint renders it. The terse clause tovati bal-alekha (literally "my good is not beyond You") expresses that the psalmist has no welfare apart from the LORD.
notes.15:3: The Hebrew syntax is compressed: the pronoun hemmah ("they") closes the relative clause "who are in the land," and the plural construct addirei ("the noble ones") is linked directly to the following clause "all my delight is in them."
notes.15:4: The Qal perfect maharu comes from mahar ("acquire by marriage-price, espouse," cf. Exod 22:15), whereas the homonymous root meaning "hurry" appears elsewhere in Biblical Hebrew only in the Piel or Niphal; "god" is implied by Hebrew acher ("another").
notes.15:6: Hebrew nachalat exhibits an archaic poetic feminine singular ending, and the Qal perfect shaferah ("is lovely," with alay "to me") is the sole verbal occurrence in Biblical Hebrew of shafar, cognate with Aramaic shefar ("be pleasing").
notes.15:10: Hebrew chasid ("devoted one") derives from chesed (covenant loyalty), distinct from qedoshim ("holy ones") in 15:3. Hebrew shachat denotes the "pit" of the underworld parallel to Sheol (from shuach, "sink down"), though ancient versions including the Septuagint linked it to shachat ("corrupt, destroy") and rendered "corruption/decay."
notes.16:4: Hebrew shamarti ("I have kept/guarded") is used here in the sense of "guard against" or "keep away from."
notes.16:10: Hebrew "their fat" (chelbamo) is a poetic idiom for a callous, unfeeling heart closed against compassion.
notes.16:11: Qere reads "they have surrounded us" (sebabunu), matching "our steps"; ketiv reads "they have surrounded me" (sebabuni).
notes.16:13: Hebrew literally reads "Your sword" (and "Your hand" in 16:14) without a preposition, understood here instrumentally ("by Your sword," "by Your hand"), though it may also be taken in apposition to the wicked.
notes.16:14: Qere reads a Qal passive participle (tzefunekha, "what You have stored up"); ketiv has an alternate spelling of the noun (tzefinekha).
notes.17:2: Hebrew erchamkha is the sole Qal occurrence of the root r-ch-m (elsewhere Piel or Pual, "have compassion"), expressing deep, heartfelt love.
notes.17:15: Hebrew rab may be parsed as a Qal perfect of r-b-b II ("shot/hurled," parallel to "sent out His arrows") or as an adjective or verb from r-b-b I ("in abundance/multiplied").
notes.17:27: Four Hithpael verbs in 17:26-27 express God's reciprocal dealing; titpattal literally means "show Yourself twisting/tortuous," that is, outmaneuvering the crooked shrewdly.
notes.17:36: Hebrew anvatekha literally means "Your humility" or "Your gentleness," denoting God's gracious condescension toward the psalmist.
notes.17:46: Hebrew yachregu is a hapax legomenon, understood from Aramaic cognates and context as "come quaking" or "emerge trembling."
notes.18:5: The Masoretic Text reads qavvam ("their measuring line," from qav), denoting the reach of the heavens' witness across the earth. Ancient versions such as the Septuagint reflect qolam ("their voice"), but the translation follows the Hebrew text.
notes.18:13: The rare noun shegi'ot (from shagah, "go astray") denotes inadvertent or unwitting errors, paired with the Niphal participle nistarot ("hidden things/faults"). The Piel imperative naqqeni ("absolve me," from naqah) is a forensic term meaning to declare innocent or free from guilt.
notes.18:14: The plural substantive zedim literally means "insolent/presumptuous ones" and elsewhere denotes arrogant people; here it is rendered "presumptuous deeds" in contrast with the inadvertent errors of v. 13, though it may alternatively refer to insolent people. The form 'etam is a Qal imperfect 1cs from tamam ("be complete/blameless"), echoing temimah ("flawless") in v. 8.
notes.18:15: The idiom hayah leratson ("be for acceptance / find acceptance") draws on sacrificial language for an offering accepted before the LORD (cf. Exod 28:38; Lev 1:3).
notes.19:4: The Piel imperfect yedashsheneh (from dashen, "be fat/rich," with the emphatic ending -eh) literally means "regard as fat/rich," an idiom for accepting a burnt offering with favor, or possibly "reduce to ashes."
notes.19:6: The Qal imperfect nidgol (from dagal, denominative of degel, "banner/standard") means "raise banners" as a sign of allegiance and victory in God's name.
notes.19:8: The Hiphil imperfect nazkir (from zakar, "remember") with the preposition be- means "make mention of," "invoke," or "boast in," and is understood by ellipsis across the first two clauses.
notes.19:10: Following the Masoretic accentuation, which places the main pause after hoshi'ah ("save!"), "the King" serves as the subject of "answer us," referring to the LORD. Some ancient versions instead take "the king" as the direct object of "save."
notes.20:2: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv has the full Qal imperfect form yagil, while the read qere has the shortened form yagel (both from gil, "exult/rejoice," with identical sense in this exclamation).
notes.20:7: The Hebrew literally reads "You make him blessings forever" (Qal imperfect of shit with double accusative), an idiom signifying both that the king is richly blessed and that he serves as an enduring channel of blessing.
notes.20:9: Verses 9-13 shift to address the king directly (hence lowercase "you/your"), as indicated by the third-person reference to the LORD in v. 10 and the renewed direct address to the LORD in v. 14; some interpreters instead read these verses as addressed to the LORD.
notes.20:13: The clause literally reads "you will set them [as] a shoulder/back" (shekhem), an idiom for putting enemies to flight. The Polel imperfect tekhonen (from kun) denotes making ready or aiming arrows upon the bowstrings.
notes.21:2: The masculine singular adjective "far" (rachoq) continues the opening question addressed to God, with "why" carried over elliptically. "My roaring" (sha'agati) literally denotes a lion's roar, anticipating the roaring lion of verse 14.
notes.21:9: Hebrew gol (Qal imperative or infinitive absolute of galal, "to roll") is an idiom for rolling one's burden onto the LORD, i.e., entrusting oneself to Him. If read as an infinitive absolute substituting for a finite verb, the opening clause means "He entrusted himself to the LORD."
notes.21:17: The Masoretic Hebrew reads ka'ari ("like a lion"), leaving the verb elliptical in the third clause. Ancient versions including the Septuagint and a Judean Desert scroll fragment reflect a verbal reading ("they pierced" or "they dug").
notes.21:22: The Masoretic Hebrew ends the verse with the Qal perfect verb anitani ("You have answered me"), marking the abrupt shift from lament to praise in verses 23-32.
notes.21:30: Translates the Masoretic Hebrew aklu ("eat," echoing verse 27) and dishne-erets (literally "fat ones of the earth," meaning the thriving or prosperous). The closing clause reads literally "and his soul he has not kept alive" (Piel perfect of chayah).
notes.22:1: This is Hebrew/MT Psalm 23 (Saints and Greek/Latin numbering: Psalm 22). The superscription mizmor ledawid is part of verse 1 in the Hebrew.
notes.22:2: Menuchoth, literally "rests," describes waters where one can rest.
notes.22:3: Nafshi yeshovev is literally "He brings back my soul (life)," meaning He restores or revives it. Ma'gele-tsedeq are "tracks" or "paths of righteousness," which can also mean the right paths.
notes.22:4: The Masoretic pointing tsalmaweth reads as a compound of tsel ("shadow") and maweth ("death"), rendered "death's shadow"; many scholars instead read tsalmuth, "deep darkness." Ra means evil or harm.
notes.22:5: Dishanta is literally "You have made fat"; with oil it means to anoint lavishly. Rewayah means "saturation, overflowing."
notes.22:6: Radaf means "pursue" or "chase." Chesed is rendered "loyal love," love that keeps covenant. The pointing weshavti looks like "and I will return" (from shuv), but with "in the house" and "for length of days" it is usually taken as a form of yashav, "dwell"; that sense is followed here. Le'orekh yamim is literally "for length of days," meaning for a long life or forever.
notes.23:4: The Hebrew text reads nafshi ("My soul"), shifting momentarily to God's own voice in the oath idiom of lifting up God's life or name to falsehood (cf. Exod 20:7). The traditional Masoretic Qere reads nafsho ("his soul").
notes.23:6: The form dorashav combines the consonantal Ketiv (singular) with the Qere vowels (plural, "those seeking Him"). The Masoretic text reads simply "Jacob" in apposition to the seeking generation, without "God of," which the Septuagint and Syriac supply.
notes.23:9: Unlike verse 7, which uses the Niphal imperative of nasa ("be raised up"), verse 9 uses the Qal imperative (se'u, "raise [them] up").
notes.24:11: The weqatal form vesalachta ("forgive") functions with imperative force following the prepositional phrase, and causal ki ("because it is great") grounds the plea in the sheer magnitude of the guilt.
notes.24:12: The third-person imperfect yivchar ("he ought to choose") is syntactically ambiguous in Hebrew and can refer either to the way the God-fearer should choose or to the way the LORD chooses.
notes.24:17: The Hiphil perfect hirchivu ("have expanded," from rachav, "be wide") is retained from the Masoretic text rather than emended to an imperative ("relieve"), creating a stark wordplay with "distresses" (literally "narrow places") and "anguish" (literally "constrictions").
notes.24:18: This psalm is an alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew; verses 18 and 19 both open with re'eh ("See," letter resh) in place of qof, and verse 22 adds a closing petition beginning with pe.
notes.25:2: The Ketiv writes a plene form with waw (tsrwph), while the Qere reads the lengthened Qal imperative tsorfah ("refine"), a metallurgical verb for smelting and purifying metal. Literally "my kidneys and my heart," referring to the seat of deepest emotions and thoughts.
notes.25:4: Hebrew na'alamim is a Niphal participle of 'lm ("be concealed"), literally "those who conceal themselves," describing hypocrites or dissemblers who hide their true character.
notes.25:9: Hebrew te'esoph (Qal jussive of 'sp) literally means "gather," used idiomatically for gathering up or sweeping a life away in death.
notes.26:4: Hebrew lebaqqer (Piel infinitive construct of bqr) can mean to inquire, inspect carefully, or contemplate in the sanctuary.
notes.26:8: The Masoretic Hebrew is famously elliptical, combining "concerning/for You" (leka) with the plural Piel imperative "Seek My face" (baqqeshu panay). The psalmist's heart recalls God's own command to His people and responds directly in the second clause.
notes.26:13: Hebrew lule ("if not") is marked in the Masoretic text with extraordinary dots above and below the letters indicating textual uncertainty, and the verse breaks off as an unfinished conditional sentence (aposiopesis) leaving the consequence unspoken.
notes.26:14: Hebrew ya'amets is a Hiphil jussive of 'mts used intransitively ("show strength, be resolute") with "your heart" as subject, paralleling the preceding Qal imperative "be strong."
notes.27:2: Hebrew debir denotes the inner sanctuary (the Holy of Holies) of the temple, toward which the psalmist raises his hands in prayer.
notes.27:7: Hebrew 'ahodennu is an uncommon poetic Hiphil imperfect of ydh ("give thanks") that retains the stem he rather than eliding it.
notes.27:8: The Masoretic Hebrew reads lamo ("for them"), referring to God's people anticipated in v. 9; some ancient versions (including the Septuagint and Syriac) read le'ammo ("for His people").
notes.28:1: Literally "sons of gods" or "sons of mighty ones," a poetic idiom for heavenly beings of the divine court.
notes.28:9: The Polel verb literally means "causes does to writhe in birth" (from the same root as the Hiphil verb in v. 8), following the Masoretic vocalization for "does" rather than an emendation to "oaks."
notes.28:10: The Hebrew noun for "flood" occurs elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible only for the Genesis flood; the sequence from perfect ("sat enthroned") to imperfect-consecutive ("sits enthroned") contrasts the LORD's past triumph with His eternal reign.
notes.29:4: Following the qere (read form), a Qal infinitive construct with first-person suffix ("from my going down to the pit"); the ketiv (written form) reads a plural participle, "from among those who go down to the pit."
notes.29:5: Literally "the memorial of His holiness," referring to the holy name by which the LORD is invoked and remembered.
notes.29:8: Literally "You caused strength to stand for my mountain," an image of God establishing the psalmist in unshakable security.
notes.29:13: The Masoretic Text reads simply "glory" without a possessive suffix; here it is a poetic term for one's inner self or being, understood from the context as "my glory."
notes.30:7: Literally "vanities of emptiness," an idiom for worthless idols. The Masoretic Text reads first-person "I hate," whereas some ancient versions read "You hate."
notes.30:11: Following the Masoretic Text, "because of my iniquity"; some ancient versions reflect a different vocalization, "because of my affliction."
notes.30:21: The Hebrew noun rendered "plots" occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and derives from a root meaning "to bind together," hence leagues or conspiracies.
notes.30:22: The Hebrew phrase can mean either "in a besieged city," pointing to the crisis from which the LORD delivered the psalmist, or "in a fortified city," as a metaphor for divine protection.
notes.31:1: Maskil is a Hebrew musical or literary term derived from the root for giving insight, echoed in the verb 'give you insight' in verse 8. Hebrew nesuy-pesha literally means 'one lifted away of transgression,' from the verb nasa ('lift/carry away,' idiomatically 'forgive').
notes.31:4: Hebrew leshaddi refers to moisture or vital sap, and becharvonei qayits combines the preposition 'in/by' with a plural noun from the root for dryness or drought to express the parching heat of summer.
notes.31:6: Hebrew le'et metso literally reads 'at a time of finding,' using the Qal infinitive construct of matsa ('find'), commonly understood as a time when God can be found.
notes.31:8: The speaker shifts here to the first person singular; most interpreters understand the LORD as replying to the psalmist, though some read the psalmist as addressing listeners in the voice of a wisdom teacher.
notes.31:9: The Hebrew syntax of the second half is terse and difficult: edyo ('its trappings' or 'its ornament,' taken by some as 'its temper') is paired with the rare Qal infinitive livlom ('to curb/restrain') and bal qerov elekha (literally 'not coming near to you').
notes.32:7: The Masoretic Hebrew reads kanned ('like a mound/heap,' as in Exodus 15:8), whereas the Septuagint and Syriac reflect a different vocalization meaning 'in a wineskin/jar.'
notes.32:14: Hebrew shivto ('His dwelling/sitting') shares the same verbal root yashav with yoshvei ('those who inhabit') at the end of the verse, contrasting the LORD's heavenly throne with all earth's dwellers.
notes.32:16: Hebrew chayil denotes military force or might here and again in verse 17 for the horse's strength, linking human armies and warhorses as inadequate sources of rescue.
notes.33:1: Hebrew beshannoto et-ta'mo literally means 'when he changed his taste/judgment,' an idiom for feigning madness (compare 1 Samuel 21:13-14, where the king of Gath is named Achish while Abimelech appears here as a Philistine royal name or title). The root ta'am ('taste/judgment') is echoed in 'Taste' in verse 9.
notes.33:6: The Masoretic Hebrew reads third-person plural perfect verbs ('They looked ... and became radiant') followed by a negated jussive ('may their faces not be ashamed'), whereas some ancient versions read second-person imperatives.
notes.33:11: The Masoretic Hebrew reads kefirim ('young lions') with rashu ('become poor/destitute'), portraying even powerful predators going hungry; the Septuagint and Syriac instead render kefirim as 'the rich.'
notes.33:18: The Masoretic Hebrew begins simply with the third-person plural verb tsa'aqu ('They cried out'), referring back to the righteous of verse 16; some ancient versions insert 'the righteous' as an explicit subject.
notes.33:23: Verses 2 through 22 form a Hebrew alphabetic acrostic (omitting a separate line for the letter vav), and verse 23 adds a closing redemption line beginning with the letter pe.
notes.34:3: The word segor is pointed in the Masoretic Text as a Qal imperative of sagar ("shut" or "bar [the way]"), though some lexicons understand it as a noun denoting a weapon such as a javelin or battle-axe.
notes.34:7: In the Masoretic Text, shachat rishtam ("pit of their net" or "their net in a pit") stands before the midpoint pause, leaving the object ("a pit") implied with the verb chafru ("they dug") in the second clause.
notes.34:13: The idiom "my prayer would return to my chest" may describe either praying with head bowed low onto the chest in grief or a prayer of blessing returning to the one who offered it.
notes.34:15: The rare plural noun nekim ("wretches") derives from nakah ("strike") and is understood either passively as abject outcasts or actively as assailants.
notes.34:16: The obscure phrase bechanfei laagei maog (literally "as godless ones of mockers of a cake") is widely taken to refer to table-parasites who deride others for a scrap of bread; charoq ("gnashed") is a Qal infinitive absolute functioning as a finite verb.
notes.35:2: The Masoretic Text reads "within my heart" (libbi), indicating that deep within himself the psalmist perceives an oracle (neum, normally a prophetic term) of transgression concerning the wicked; some ancient versions read "his heart."
notes.35:3: Literally "for he makes smooth to himself in his eyes, to find his iniquity, to hate," a compressed clause expressing how the wicked smoothly reassures himself concerning his guilt being detected and hated, or flatters himself until it is exposed.
notes.35:7: The construct phrase harrei-el ("God's mountains") serves in Hebrew both literally and as a superlative idiom for towering, mighty mountains.
notes.36:1: The verb rendered 'become agitated' is the Hithpael jussive of harah ('burn, become hot'), literally 'do not heat yourself up,' recurring in verses 7 and 8.
notes.36:3: The clause 'feed on faithfulness' translates the Qal imperative of ra'ah ('graze, feed'), though it may also denote tending or cultivating faithfulness.
notes.36:20: The phrase 'splendor of meadows' takes karim as pastures or meadows (echoing the withering grass in verse 2); alternatively, karim can mean 'lambs,' depicting burnt portions vanishing in smoke.
notes.36:35: The participle 'spreading himself out' is Hithpael of arah, and the noun rendered 'native tree' (ezrah) literally means 'a native,' here a tree rooted in its own soil.
notes.36:36: The Masoretic Text has the third-person verb 'he passed away,' shifting to the first-person 'I sought him' in the second half of the verse.
notes.37:1: The heading 'to bring to remembrance' translates the Hiphil infinitive construct of zakar, likely a liturgical designation for invoking God's remembrance or accompanying a memorial offering.
notes.37:8: The word 'burning' translates the Niphal participle of qalah ('roast, parch'), describing feverish inflammation in the flanks.
notes.37:11: The verb 'pounds' is a rare reduplicated Pealal form of sahar ('go around'), depicting a palpitating heart; the plural pronoun translated 'even that' refers loosely back to the light of the eyes.
notes.37:20: The Masoretic Text reads hayyim ('living, vigorous'), contrasting the vitality of the psalmist's enemies with his own weakened condition.
notes.37:21: Ketiv reads a fuller orthographic spelling (rdwpy) and Qere reads rodfi (Qal infinitive construct of radaph with first-person suffix, 'my pursuing'); the translation follows the Qere with no difference in sense.
notes.38:1: Ketiv reads "Jedithun" while Qere reads "Jeduthun", a Levitical music leader under David; the translation follows the Qere.
notes.38:3: The Hebrew phrase "kept silent from good" is terse, conveying either refraining even from speaking good words or keeping silent with no good result.
notes.38:11: The Hebrew noun translated "assault" occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and derives from a root denoting hostility or striking.
notes.38:14: The imperative translated "Look away" is a shortened form associated with turning the gaze away, followed by a Hiphil cohortative meaning "brighten up" or "recover cheerfulness."
notes.39:4: The Hebrew pairs two nearly homophonous Qal imperfect verbs, "see" and "fear/be in awe", creating a deliberate sound play.
notes.39:6: The clause "there is no comparing to You" renders a concise idiom combining the negative particle with the Qal infinitive construct of a verb meaning "to set in order" or "to compare."
notes.39:7: The Masoretic Hebrew reads literally "ears You have dug for me", a metaphor for opening attentive, obedient ears; the Septuagint instead reads "a body You prepared for me."
notes.39:12: The Hebrew uses the indicative negation with the Qal imperfect ("will not hold back"), expressing confidence in God's ongoing mercy, though some take it as a plea ("do not withhold").
notes.40:3: Ketiv reads an imperfect passive form ("he will be called blessed"), whereas Qere reads a Pual weqatal ("and he will be pronounced blessed"); the translation follows the Qere. The clause "do not hand him over" abruptly shifts to second-person address to God, and "desire" literally translates Hebrew "soul/appetite."
notes.40:4: Literally "all his bed You turn/transform in his sickness", an idiom denoting either tending a sick person's bed or transforming their illness into recovery, again shifting to second-person address to God.
notes.40:9: The Hebrew phrase "a ruinous thing" (literally "a thing of worthlessness/destruction") is paired with the Qal passive participle "poured into him", picturing a lethal affliction or curse fixed upon the sufferer.
notes.40:10: "My close companion" renders the Hebrew idiom "the man of my peace", denoting a trusted ally, and "has raised his heel high" literally renders the Hiphil verb "has magnified the heel", an image of treacherous betrayal.
notes.41:2: Hebrew ayyal (deer) is grammatically masculine singular while the verb ta'arog (yearns) is feminine singular, likely treating the noun as epicene or referring to a doe; afiqei-mayim literally denotes channels or watercourses of water.
notes.41:3: The Masoretic vocalization points we'era'eh as a Niphal (appear), taking penei elohim adverbially as before the face of God, whereas the unvocalized consonants could also be read as Qal (see the face of God).
notes.41:5: Hebrew bassakh (in the throng) is a biblical hapax legomenon; eddaddem is an unusual Hithpael imperfect of dadah (walk slowly/in procession) with an attached third-person plural suffix, meaning either walking in procession with them or leading them in procession.
notes.41:6: The Masoretic text literally reads yeshu'ot panav (the salvations/deliverances of His face, i.e., His presence) and places elohai (My God) at the beginning of 41:7, contrasting with the refrains at 41:12 and 42:5 which read yeshu'ot panai welohai (the deliverance of my face and my God).
notes.41:8: Hebrew tsinnorekha is the plural of the rare noun tsinnor (water-channel, cataract, or cascade), occurring elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible only in 2 Samuel 5:8.
notes.42:2: Hebrew ethallekh uses the iterative/reflexive Hithpael stem of halakh (walk about), distinguishing this lament from the Qal verb elekh (go) in the parallel verse at 41:10.
notes.42:4: Hebrew simchat gili (literally the gladness of my rejoicing) is a construct phrase combining two near-synonymous nouns for superlative emphasis (my highest joy).
notes.43:3: Hiphil horashta (dispossessed) forms a deliberate wordplay with Qal yaresho (possess) in 43:4; Piel watteshallechem (made them spread out) continues the vine-planting image of wattitta'em (planted them) with Israel as object, though some take it as sent them away referring to the peoples.
notes.43:13: Hebrew belo-hon literally means for no wealth, and Piel ribbitah (increased/raised high) with bimchireihem (in their prices) expresses that God set no high price and sought no gain in selling His people.
notes.43:19: The negative lo in the first clause carries double-duty force into the second clause (nor have our steps turned aside), where the third-person feminine singular wayyiqtol verb wattett (Qal of natah) agrees with feminine ashureinu (our steps).
notes.43:20: Hebrew ki functions adversatively or concessively here (Yet) following the protestation of loyalty in 43:18-19; the Masoretic pointing tsalmawet treats the noun as shadow of death, while the consonantal form likely means deep darkness, captured here by deathly shadow.
notes.43:27: Hebrew ezratah is a poetic lengthened form of ezrah (help) with the emphatic ending -atah, standing directly after the imperative qumah (Rise up).
notes.44:1: Shoshannim ("Lilies," translated in 69:1 and 80:1 [Saints 68:1, 79:1]) likely denotes a melody or musical setting. Maskil, a Hiphil participle of the root skl, designates a contemplative or skillful poem.
notes.44:5: The Hebrew pairs two Qal imperatives without a conjunction, succeed and ride forth, and joins humility and righteousness with a maqqef in an unusual absolute-noun compound, understood either as an asyndetic pair or as righteous humility.
notes.44:6: The middle clause, peoples fall beneath you, functions as a poetic parenthetical exclamation separating the subject and predicate of the arrow clause.
notes.44:7: Your throne, God renders elohim as a direct vocative, as in the ancient versions, though some interpreters construe the phrase as Your divine throne.
notes.44:9: The form minni is taken as a poetic plural of men, stringed instruments, as in Psalm 150:4; alternatively it may be a poetic form of the preposition min with an indefinite subject.
notes.45:1: Alamoth literally means young women or maidens, a musical term found also in 1 Chronicles 15:20 that likely indicates a high vocal register or soprano accompaniment.
notes.45:2: Literally a help in distresses He is exceedingly found; the masculine Niphal form nimtsa agrees with God rather than the feminine noun help, stressing that God proves abundantly present in trouble.
notes.45:3: The Hiphil infinitive construct hamir, from the root mwr meaning to change or exchange, is used intransitively here for the earth undergoing upheaval or giving way.
notes.45:10: Hebrew agalot literally denotes wagons or war-carts, distinct from the usual word for chariots; the Septuagint translates the term as shields.
notes.45:11: Desist translates the Hiphil imperative harpu, literally let drop or slacken one's hands. The repeated verb arum is Qal, expressing God's own rising high in exaltation.
notes.46:4: The rare Hiphil verb yadber, from dbr II meaning to subdue or bring under as in Psalm 18:48 MT, is distinct from the common Piel verb meaning to speak.
notes.46:8: Make music renders the Piel imperative of zmr, repeated four times in verse 7 and cognate to psalm in verse 1. Maskil, as in 44:1, may denote the psalm genre or serve adverbially as skillfully.
notes.46:10: The Masoretic Text reads am, as the people of the God of Abraham, whereas the Septuagint and Syriac vocalize the consonants as im, with the God of Abraham. Shields of the earth is a metaphor for earthly rulers and defenders.
notes.47:3: The noun נוֹף ('height, elevation') is a Hebrew hapax legomenon, and יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן literally means 'the flanks/recesses of the north,' also evoking the northern mountain Zaphon.
notes.47:14: פַּסְּגוּ is a Piel imperative hapax legomenon meaning 'pass through' or 'inspect closely.'
notes.47:15: The Masoretic text divides עַל־מוּת into two words ('to/beyond death,' with מוּת pointed as the infinitive construct); some read it as a single word meaning 'forever' or as a musical direction.
notes.48:3: בְּנֵי אָדָם ('sons of mankind') and בְּנֵי־אִישׁ ('sons of a man [of rank]') form a Hebrew idiom contrasting ordinary people with those of high standing.
notes.48:6: עֲקֵבַי is ambiguous and can mean either 'my deceivers/supplanters' (from the root עקב, linking to the plural participle in v. 7) or 'my heels' (i.e., 'iniquity at my heels').
notes.48:8: Translates the Masoretic text אָח ('a brother'); some ancient versions and commentators emend to אַךְ ('surely').
notes.48:12: Translates the Masoretic text קִרְבָּם ('their inward thought'); the Septuagint and Syriac reflect transposed consonants קִבְרָם ('their graves').
notes.48:15: Ketiv וצירם ('their image') vs. Qere וְצוּרָם ('their form/shape'); the translation follows the Qere. The closing phrase מִזְּבֻל לוֹ literally means 'away from a dwelling for it,' i.e., far from its dwelling.
notes.49:11: זִיז שָׂדַי pairs the rare noun זִיז ('moving creatures') with the poetic form שָׂדַי ('field'), and עִמָּדִי literally means 'with Me.'
notes.49:18: וַתִּרֶץ is the apocopated Qal wayyiqtol of רָצָה ('be pleased with, agree/associate with'), rather than רוּץ ('run,' reflected in some ancient versions).
notes.49:20: תִּתֶּן־דֹּפִי literally means 'you put a blemish/fault,' using the hapax legomenon דֹּפִי ('blemish, slander').
notes.49:23: וְשָׂם דֶּרֶךְ is a compressed Masoretic expression literally meaning 'and sets a way,' understood as directing or ordering one's conduct.
notes.50:4: Ketiv writes the Hiphil infinitive absolute harbeh, while Qere reads the shortened Hiphil imperative herev from rabah, meaning "multiply"; here it functions adverbially with the following imperative to express thorough or repeated washing.
notes.50:8: The rare plural noun tuhot, translated "inward parts," occurs only here and in Job 38:36; it likely derives from the root tuah, meaning "cover over," and denotes the hidden inner self.
notes.50:9: The verb translated "Cleanse me from sin" is a privative Piel of hata, "to sin," meaning "to de-sin" or purify ritually from sin, as in purification rites with hyssop in Numbers 19:19.
notes.50:13: Hebrew ruach qodshekha literally means "the spirit of Your holiness" (parallel to ruach qodsho in Isa 63:10–11).
notes.50:14: The verb tismekeni can be parsed either as third feminine singular with "a willing spirit" as subject, translated here, or as second masculine singular addressed to God with "a willing spirit" as an instrumental accusative.
notes.51:3: The second clause is a terse verbless statement in the Masoretic Text, literally "God's loyal love all day long," contrasting God's ongoing faithfulness with the warrior's boasting.
notes.51:7: The verb shereshka is a privative Piel of shoresh, "root," meaning "to pull up by the roots," forming a sharp contrast with the lush olive tree in verse 10.
notes.51:9: The noun hawwato, translated "his ruin," repeats the root hawwot from verse 4; it can denote either destructive calamity or, from a homonymous root, greedy desire.
notes.51:11: Translates the Masoretic verb aqawweh, Piel of qawah meaning "to wait or hope for," rather than emending the text to "proclaim."
notes.52:1: Mahalath is an uncertain musical or liturgical heading, appearing also in the superscription of Psalm 88 MT, likely naming a tune or instrument.
notes.52:5: The first-person suffix in "My people" introduces God's own voice even though the next clause refers to God in the third person, a shift common in prophetic and poetic speech.
notes.52:6: This verse diverges notably from its parallel in Psalm 14:5-6 MT, featuring a triple repetition of the root pahad, "dread," and announcing the scattering of the besieger's bones.
notes.52:7: "If only ... would come" renders the Hebrew optative idiom mi yitten, literally "who will give," and "salvation" translates an intensive plural yeshuot, literally "deliverances."
notes.53:6: The phrase literally reads 'among those who sustain my life' (beth essentiae with a plural Qal participle of samakh), an idiom expressing that the Lord is the preeminent sustainer of the psalmist's life.
notes.53:7: The Qere reads Hiphil yashiv ('He will turn back' the evil), whereas the Ketiv reads Qal yashuv ('the evil will return' upon my foes).
notes.53:9: The Hebrew idiom 'my eye has looked upon' (Qal of ra'ah with the preposition be-) denotes gazing upon defeated enemies in vindication or triumph.
notes.54:3: The rare Hiphil verb 'arid (from rud) denotes restless roaming or agitation, paired with the Hiphil cohortative 'ahimah (from hum, 'be in turmoil, groan aloud').
notes.54:16: The Qere reads two words, yashi mavet (defective Hiphil jussive of nasha' II, 'deceive/come unawares,' plus 'death'), whereas the Ketiv writes a single plural noun yeshimot ('desolations').
notes.54:19: Literally 'for in/as many they were with me' (beth essentiae with rabbim and 'immadi), where 'with me' in a battle context carries the adversarial sense 'engaged against me,' though some interpret it as 'on my side.'
notes.54:20: MT vocalizes veya'anem as Qal of 'anah I ('and answer them,' i.e., in judgment), whereas some ancient versions read Piel ('humble/afflict them'). Literally 'there are no changes for them' (chalifot) indicates that they do not reform or experience humbling reversals.
notes.54:22: MT vocalizes a plural verb chalqu with the hapax plural noun machama'ot ('buttery utterances/things of his mouth'), whereas revocalizing the noun as a comparative would give 'smoother than butter,' parallel to 'softer than oil.'
notes.55:1: The obscure musical heading yonat 'elem rechoqim literally reads 'dove of silence of distant places' in MT; an alternative vocalization 'elim would mean 'terebinths/oaks.'
notes.55:3: The noun marom ('height, loftiness') is taken here adverbially ('haughtily/proudly'), though some construe it as a vocative divine title ('Most High' or 'Exalted One').
notes.55:7: The Qere reads Qal yitsponu ('they lie hidden/lurk'), whereas the Ketiv reads Hiphil yatspinu ('they conceal' or 'set an ambush').
notes.55:8: MT literally reads 'because of iniquity, escape for them' (using the noun/infinitive pallet, 'escape,' as in Ps 32:7 MT), understood here as an unmarked rhetorical question.
notes.55:9: The Hebrew employs a double wordplay linking nodi ('my wandering') with no'dekha ('Your wineskin') and safartah ('You have counted') with sifratekha ('Your register/record').
notes.56:4: The Piel perfect cheref ("puts to shame" or "reproaches") is taken with God as subject and the Qal participle sho'afi ("the one who tramples on me" or "pants after me") as object; alternatively, the clause may be read circumstantially as "though the one who tramples on me taunts."
notes.56:5: The Qal active participle lohatim literally means "blazing ones" or "fiery ones," used metaphorically for fierce, devouring enemies in apposition to "sons of men."
notes.56:7: The Masoretic Text reads the singular Qal perfect kafaf ("bowed low"), taken intransitively with "my soul" as subject (or impersonally, "my soul was bowed down"), rather than the plural verb found in some ancient versions.
notes.57:2: The Masoretic vocalization reads the noun elem ("silence"), functioning adverbially ("in silence") as an ironic rebuke of unjust judges; the consonants can also be revocalized as elim ("gods" or "mighty ones").
notes.57:8: The Niphal yimma'asu derives from a by-form of masas ("melt away"). In the difficult second clause, chitsav is a defectively spelled plural ("his arrows") and yitmolalu is a Hithpolel ("be cut off" or "wither," suggesting blunted or broken arrows); the subject of "aims" is taken as the individual wicked enemy, though some read God as subject.
notes.57:9: Both shablul ("snail" or "slug") and temes ("dissolution" or "melting") occur only here in the Hebrew Bible. The plural verb chazu ("have seen") agrees either collectively with the singular nefel ("miscarriage") or directly with the plural wicked of the preceding verse.
notes.57:10: This compressed image compares sudden judgment to a whirlwind sweeping away thorn-fuel before cooking pots can feel its heat (literally "perceive the bramble"). The correlative kemo-chai kemo-charon ("whether green or ablaze") may alternatively mean "while alive, in fierce wrath," with the masculine singular suffix on yis'arennu ("sweep it away") referring either to the bramble or collectively to the wicked.
notes.57:12: The Qal participle shoftim ("judges") is grammatically plural in agreement with the plural form of Elohim ("God"), though referring here to God.
notes.58:10: The Masoretic Text reads uzzo ("his strength"), taken adverbially of the enemy's power ("Because of his strength I will keep watch for You"), whereas verse 18 and some manuscripts and ancient versions read uzzi ("my strength").
notes.58:11: Ketiv reads chasdo ("His loyal love"), while the Qere followed here reads chasdi ("my loyal love," matching verse 18). The Hiphil yar'eni with the preposition be ("let me look upon") idiomatically denotes looking upon foes in vindication or triumph.
notes.58:13: The opening phrases lack an explicit preposition and are taken causally ("For the sin of their mouths, the word of their lips") in parallel with the prepositional phrases at the end of the verse; alternatively, they may form a nominal clause ("The sin of their mouths is the word of their lips").
notes.58:16: Ketiv reads Qal yanu'un ("they wander"), while the Qere followed here reads Hiphil yeni'un (used intransitively, "they wander about," echoing the Hiphil of the same root in verse 12). The final verb vayyalinu matches the Qal form of lin ("spend the night"), though the Septuagint connects it to lun ("grumble").
notes.59:4: The verb translated 'cracked it open' (Hebrew patsam, Qal) occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes splitting or cleaving apart. 'Heal' renders refah, a Qal imperative of rafa spelled with a final he instead of aleph.
notes.59:6: The Masoretic text pairs nes ('banner') with the Hithpolel infinitive lehithnoses ('to be lifted high / raised as a banner') and reads the rare noun qoshet ('truth'). Some ancient versions presuppose a different Hebrew word meaning 'bow' and derive the verb from 'flee.'
notes.59:7: The translation follows the read text (qere, 'and answer me'). The written text (ketiv) reads 'and answer us.'
notes.59:10: The Masoretic text addresses Philistia directly with a second-person feminine singular Hithpolel imperative ('over Me, Philistia, shout in triumph!'), likely ironic in tone, whereas a parallel psalm elsewhere in the Psalter has a first-person singular verb.
notes.60:1: Hebrew neginat is a singular feminine form ('a stringed instrument'), perhaps preserving an archaic absolute ending or serving as a construct before 'of David.'
notes.60:3: Hebrew yarum mimmenni literally means 'that is high beyond me' (or 'higher than I'), indicating a lofty refuge inaccessible without God's help.
notes.60:8: Hebrew man is an apocopated Piel imperative singular of manah ('appoint, assign'), calling on God to commission loyal love and truth as guardians of the king.
notes.61:2: The noun dumiyyah ('stillness, silence') stands in deliberate contrast with the Qal feminine singular imperative dommi ('be still!') in 61:6. The particle akh ('only') recurs six times in this psalm (verses 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10) as a unifying refrain.
notes.61:4: The Poel verb tehotetu ('assail') is a biblical hapax legomenon. The translation follows the vocalization of the critical text, teratsechu, a Piel active ('you batter/murder'); an alternate vocalization tradition (Ben Naphtali) reads a Pual passive ('you will be slain'). The simile of the leaning wall describes the man under attack.
notes.61:5: Hebrew befiv literally reads 'with his mouth' (a distributive singular suffix paired with the plural verb 'they bless'), meaning each adversary blesses with his own mouth.
notes.61:10: The parallel idioms 'sons of mankind' (bene-adam) and 'sons of man' (bene-ish) encompass all humanity, from the lowly to the prominent. The final clause uses comparative min elliptically with hevel ('less than a breath,' i.e., lighter than a puff of air).
notes.62:2: The verb translated "pines" (kamah) is a hapax legomenon in Biblical Hebrew, expressing fainting or intense longing. The masculine singular adjective ayeph ("weary") stands in grammatical tension with the feminine construct phrase erets-tsiyyah ("parched land"), either treating "land" as masculine or describing the speaker's own exhaustion.
notes.62:10: The prepositional phrase leshoah ("for ruin") can describe either the enemies' destructive aim in seeking the psalmist's life or, ironically, the ruin that will fall upon themselves.
notes.62:11: The verb yaggiruhu ("they will be surrendered") is literally an impersonal third-person plural Hiphil of nagar ("pour out" or "hand over") with a collective singular object suffix ("him"), paired with the idiom al-yedey-cherev (literally "upon the hands of the sword").
notes.63:4: The verb darekhu ("aimed," from darakh, literally "tread" or "bend") is normally used for bending a bow with the foot and is extended here to aiming an arrow, which stands in direct apposition to "a bitter word."
notes.63:5: Hebrew links the verbs yarah ("shoot") and yare ("fear") in a deliberate soundplay running from "they shoot him, and they do not fear" here to God shooting them in v. 8 and all humanity fearing in v. 10.
notes.63:7: The Masoretic Text reads tamnu, first-person plural Qal perfect of tamam ("we have completed"), introducing the plotters' boast without an explicit speech verb, alongside a threefold play on the root chaphas ("search out," "plot," and Pual participle "searched-out").
notes.63:9: The form vayyakhshiluhu is a third-person plural Hiphil of kashal with a collective singular suffix (literally "they will cause him to stumble," functioning passively), followed by the nominal clause "against them is their own tongue." The Hithpolel yitnodedu ("will shake their heads") can alternatively mean "will flee away."
notes.64:2: The Masoretic Text vocalizes dumiyyah as the noun "silence" or "stillness" (literally "to You silence is praise," or "praise waits in silence for You"); some ancient versions reflect a different vocalization of the same consonants meaning "is fitting."
notes.64:6: The masculine plural adjective rechoqim ("distant ones") follows singular yam ("sea"), either modifying the preceding plural construct phrase ("the distant ends of earth and sea") or denoting "the sea of distant shores."
notes.64:11: The forms ravveh ("saturate") and nachet ("level") are Piel infinitives absolute continuing the second-person finite verbs of the preceding verse, though both forms are morphologically identical to Piel imperatives.
notes.64:12: Hebrew shenat tovatekha is literally a construct chain, "the year of Your goodness," that is, the year marked by Your goodness or bounty.
notes.65:3: The Piel verb yekachashu (from the root kachash, "to act falsely" or "deny") paired with the preposition le denotes cringing or feigning submission before a superior power.
notes.65:7: The Qere (read form) yarumu is a Qal imperfect meaning "lift themselves up" or "exalt themselves" (with the ethical dative lamo, "for themselves"), whereas the Ketiv (written form) yrymw represents a Hiphil form ("raise up").
notes.65:11: The noun muaqah ("crushing weight") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and derives from a root meaning "to press" or "squeeze."
notes.65:17: The form romam may be parsed either as a noun meaning "high praise" or as a Polal perfect ("He was extolled"); "under my tongue" is a Hebrew idiom for words kept ready on the tongue.
notes.66:2: Unlike Numbers 6:25, which uses the preposition el ("upon"), the Hebrew here uses ittanu ("with us").
notes.66:5: The verb tanchem is a Hiphil imperfect of nachah ("to lead" or "guide") with a resumptive plural object suffix referring back to the fronted "nations."
notes.67:5: The Qal imperative sollu literally means "cast up a highway," and aravot in the Masoretic text denotes "desert plains" (though some compare a cognate term for "clouds"); be-Yah shemo uses the shortened divine name Yah with the preposition be expressing identity ("His name is the LORD").
notes.67:9: The archaic expression zeh Sinai (compare Judges 5:5) literally reads "this Sinai" and functions either as a determinative title ("the One of Sinai") in apposition to God or as an emphatic exclamation ("even Sinai").
notes.67:14: This poetic verse is syntactically elliptical without a finite verb in the second clause; shefattayim is a dual noun understood as "sheepfolds" (or "hearthstones"), and yeraqraq charuts literally denotes "greenish-yellow gold," describing the sheen of fine gold.
notes.67:21: The divine name followed by Adonai reverses the usual order (Adonai followed by the divine name); the divine name carries the vowels of Elohim so that Adonai is not read twice. It is rendered here as "GOD, the Lord."
notes.67:31: The Hithpael participle mitrappes (from raphas) means "prostrating/humbling oneself" (compare Proverbs 6:3) or "trampling down," and the Masoretic text reads the Piel perfect bizzar ("He has scattered") rather than an imperative.
notes.68:2: Hebrew nefesh literally means throat or neck in drowning imagery, as well as life or soul.
notes.68:11: The Masoretic text reads literally, I wept in fasting my soul, taking my soul as an adverbial specification rather than supplying the verb humbled found in the Septuagint.
notes.68:23: The Masoretic text vocalizes lishlomim, meaning for those at peace or in their security, whereas the Septuagint reflects a different vocalization meaning for retribution.
notes.68:27: The Masoretic text reads yesapperu, Piel of sfr meaning they talk of or recount, whereas the Septuagint reflects a different verb meaning they add to.
notes.68:32: Hebrew maqrin mafris consists of two Hiphil denominative participles, literally putting forth horns and having hooves, describing a mature, ritually clean sacrificial bull.
