native_notes.58:2: The Masoretic vocalization reads the noun elem ("silence"), functioning adverbially ("in silence") as an ironic rebuke of unjust judges; the consonants can also be revocalized as elim ("gods" or "mighty ones").
native_notes.58:8: The Niphal yimma'asu derives from a by-form of masas ("melt away"). In the difficult second clause, chitsav is a defectively spelled plural ("his arrows") and yitmolalu is a Hithpolel ("be cut off" or "wither," suggesting blunted or broken arrows); the subject of "aims" is taken as the individual wicked enemy, though some read God as subject.
native_notes.58:9: Both shablul ("snail" or "slug") and temes ("dissolution" or "melting") occur only here in the Hebrew Bible. The plural verb chazu ("have seen") agrees either collectively with the singular nefel ("miscarriage") or directly with the plural wicked of the preceding verse.
native_notes.58:10: This compressed image compares sudden judgment to a whirlwind sweeping away thorn-fuel before cooking pots can feel its heat (literally "perceive the bramble"). The correlative kemo-chai kemo-charon ("whether green or ablaze") may alternatively mean "while alive, in fierce wrath," with the masculine singular suffix on yis'arennu ("sweep it away") referring either to the bramble or collectively to the wicked.
native_notes.58:12: The Qal participle shoftim ("judges") is grammatically plural in agreement with the plural form of Elohim ("God"), though referring here to God.
native_notes.59:10: The Masoretic Text reads uzzo ("his strength"), taken adverbially of the enemy's power ("Because of his strength I will keep watch for You"), whereas verse 18 and some manuscripts and ancient versions read uzzi ("my strength").
native_notes.59:11: Ketiv reads chasdo ("His loyal love"), while the Qere followed here reads chasdi ("my loyal love," matching verse 18). The Hiphil yar'eni with the preposition be ("let me look upon") idiomatically denotes looking upon foes in vindication or triumph.
native_notes.59:13: The opening phrases lack an explicit preposition and are taken causally ("For the sin of their mouths, the word of their lips") in parallel with the prepositional phrases at the end of the verse; alternatively, they may form a nominal clause ("The sin of their mouths is the word of their lips").
native_notes.59:16: Ketiv reads Qal yanu'un ("they wander"), while the Qere followed here reads Hiphil yeni'un (used intransitively, "they wander about," echoing the Hiphil of the same root in verse 12). The final verb vayyalinu matches the Qal form of lin ("spend the night"), though the Septuagint connects it to lun ("grumble").
native_notes.60:4: The verb translated 'cracked it open' (Hebrew patsam, Qal) occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes splitting or cleaving apart. 'Heal' renders refah, a Qal imperative of rafa spelled with a final he instead of aleph.
native_notes.60:6: The Masoretic text pairs nes ('banner') with the Hithpolel infinitive lehithnoses ('to be lifted high / raised as a banner') and reads the rare noun qoshet ('truth'). Some ancient versions presuppose a different Hebrew word meaning 'bow' and derive the verb from 'flee.'
native_notes.60:7: The translation follows the read text (qere, 'and answer me'). The written text (ketiv) reads 'and answer us.'
native_notes.60:10: The Masoretic text addresses Philistia directly with a second-person feminine singular Hithpolel imperative ('over Me, Philistia, shout in triumph!'), likely ironic in tone, whereas a parallel psalm elsewhere in the Psalter has a first-person singular verb.
native_notes.61:1: Hebrew neginat is a singular feminine form ('a stringed instrument'), perhaps preserving an archaic absolute ending or serving as a construct before 'of David.'
native_notes.61:3: Hebrew yarum mimmenni literally means 'that is high beyond me' (or 'higher than I'), indicating a lofty refuge inaccessible without God's help.
native_notes.61:8: Hebrew man is an apocopated Piel imperative singular of manah ('appoint, assign'), calling on God to commission loyal love and truth as guardians of the king.
native_notes.62:2: The noun dumiyyah ('stillness, silence') stands in deliberate contrast with the Qal feminine singular imperative dommi ('be still!') in 61:6. The particle akh ('only') recurs six times in this psalm (verses 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10) as a unifying refrain.
native_notes.62:4: The Poel verb tehotetu ('assail') is a biblical hapax legomenon. The translation follows the vocalization of the critical text, teratsechu, a Piel active ('you batter/murder'); an alternate vocalization tradition (Ben Naphtali) reads a Pual passive ('you will be slain'). The simile of the leaning wall describes the man under attack.
native_notes.62:5: Hebrew befiv literally reads 'with his mouth' (a distributive singular suffix paired with the plural verb 'they bless'), meaning each adversary blesses with his own mouth.
native_notes.62:10: The parallel idioms 'sons of mankind' (bene-adam) and 'sons of man' (bene-ish) encompass all humanity, from the lowly to the prominent. The final clause uses comparative min elliptically with hevel ('less than a breath,' i.e., lighter than a puff of air).
native_notes.63:2: The verb translated "pines" (kamah) is a hapax legomenon in Biblical Hebrew, expressing fainting or intense longing. The masculine singular adjective ayeph ("weary") stands in grammatical tension with the feminine construct phrase erets-tsiyyah ("parched land"), either treating "land" as masculine or describing the speaker's own exhaustion.
native_notes.63:10: The prepositional phrase leshoah ("for ruin") can describe either the enemies' destructive aim in seeking the psalmist's life or, ironically, the ruin that will fall upon themselves.
native_notes.63:11: The verb yaggiruhu ("they will be surrendered") is literally an impersonal third-person plural Hiphil of nagar ("pour out" or "hand over") with a collective singular object suffix ("him"), paired with the idiom al-yedey-cherev (literally "upon the hands of the sword").
native_notes.64:4: The verb darekhu ("aimed," from darakh, literally "tread" or "bend") is normally used for bending a bow with the foot and is extended here to aiming an arrow, which stands in direct apposition to "a bitter word."
native_notes.64:5: Hebrew links the verbs yarah ("shoot") and yare ("fear") in a deliberate soundplay running from "they shoot him, and they do not fear" here to God shooting them in v. 8 and all humanity fearing in v. 10.
native_notes.64:7: The Masoretic Text reads tamnu, first-person plural Qal perfect of tamam ("we have completed"), introducing the plotters' boast without an explicit speech verb, alongside a threefold play on the root chaphas ("search out," "plot," and Pual participle "searched-out").
native_notes.64:9: The form vayyakhshiluhu is a third-person plural Hiphil of kashal with a collective singular suffix (literally "they will cause him to stumble," functioning passively), followed by the nominal clause "against them is their own tongue." The Hithpolel yitnodedu ("will shake their heads") can alternatively mean "will flee away."
native_notes.65:2: The Masoretic Text vocalizes dumiyyah as the noun "silence" or "stillness" (literally "to You silence is praise," or "praise waits in silence for You"); some ancient versions reflect a different vocalization of the same consonants meaning "is fitting."
native_notes.65:6: The masculine plural adjective rechoqim ("distant ones") follows singular yam ("sea"), either modifying the preceding plural construct phrase ("the distant ends of earth and sea") or denoting "the sea of distant shores."
native_notes.65:11: The forms ravveh ("saturate") and nachet ("level") are Piel infinitives absolute continuing the second-person finite verbs of the preceding verse, though both forms are morphologically identical to Piel imperatives.
native_notes.65:12: Hebrew shenat tovatekha is literally a construct chain, "the year of Your goodness," that is, the year marked by Your goodness or bounty.
native_notes.66:3: The Piel verb yekachashu (from the root kachash, "to act falsely" or "deny") paired with the preposition le denotes cringing or feigning submission before a superior power.
native_notes.66:7: The Qere (read form) yarumu is a Qal imperfect meaning "lift themselves up" or "exalt themselves" (with the ethical dative lamo, "for themselves"), whereas the Ketiv (written form) yrymw represents a Hiphil form ("raise up").
native_notes.66:11: The noun muaqah ("crushing weight") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and derives from a root meaning "to press" or "squeeze."
native_notes.66:17: The form romam may be parsed either as a noun meaning "high praise" or as a Polal perfect ("He was extolled"); "under my tongue" is a Hebrew idiom for words kept ready on the tongue.
native_notes.67:2: Unlike Numbers 6:25, which uses the preposition el ("upon"), the Hebrew here uses ittanu ("with us").
native_notes.67:5: The verb tanchem is a Hiphil imperfect of nachah ("to lead" or "guide") with a resumptive plural object suffix referring back to the fronted "nations."
native_notes.68:5: The Qal imperative sollu literally means "cast up a highway," and aravot in the Masoretic text denotes "desert plains" (though some compare a cognate term for "clouds"); be-Yah shemo uses the shortened divine name Yah with the preposition be expressing identity ("His name is the LORD").
native_notes.68:9: The archaic expression zeh Sinai (compare Judges 5:5) literally reads "this Sinai" and functions either as a determinative title ("the One of Sinai") in apposition to God or as an emphatic exclamation ("even Sinai").
native_notes.68:14: This poetic verse is syntactically elliptical without a finite verb in the second clause; shefattayim is a dual noun understood as "sheepfolds" (or "hearthstones"), and yeraqraq charuts literally denotes "greenish-yellow gold," describing the sheen of fine gold.
native_notes.68:21: The divine name followed by Adonai reverses the usual order (Adonai followed by the divine name); the divine name carries the vowels of Elohim so that Adonai is not read twice. It is rendered here as "GOD, the Lord."
native_notes.68:31: The Hithpael participle mitrappes (from raphas) means "prostrating/humbling oneself" (compare Proverbs 6:3) or "trampling down," and the Masoretic text reads the Piel perfect bizzar ("He has scattered") rather than an imperative.
native_notes.69:2: Hebrew nefesh literally means throat or neck in drowning imagery, as well as life or soul.
native_notes.69:11: The Masoretic text reads literally, I wept in fasting my soul, taking my soul as an adverbial specification rather than supplying the verb humbled found in the Septuagint.
native_notes.69:23: The Masoretic text vocalizes lishlomim, meaning for those at peace or in their security, whereas the Septuagint reflects a different vocalization meaning for retribution.
native_notes.69:27: The Masoretic text reads yesapperu, Piel of sfr meaning they talk of or recount, whereas the Septuagint reflects a different verb meaning they add to.
native_notes.69:32: Hebrew maqrin mafris consists of two Hiphil denominative participles, literally putting forth horns and having hooves, describing a mature, ritually clean sacrificial bull.
native_notes.70:1: Hebrew lehazkir is a Hiphil infinitive construct of zkr, literally to cause to remember or to bring to remembrance, probably a liturgical heading.
native_notes.70:2: The final imperative chushah, hurry, governs both halves of the verse through poetic ellipsis.
native_notes.70:4: Hebrew al-eqev, literally on the heel of, is an idiom meaning on account of, and the Masoretic verb yashuvu, let them turn back, differs from the parallel psalm, which reads be appalled.
native_notes.71:3: The Masoretic text reads maon, dwelling or habitation, and tsivvita, You have commanded, whereas the Septuagint harmonizes with a similar psalm to read stronghold.
native_notes.71:6: Hebrew gozi is a rare Qal participle from guz or gazah, probably meaning the One who severed or brought me out at birth.
native_notes.71:12: Ketiv writes chishah, a rare spelling with yod, while qere reads chushah, the standard Qal imperative with paragogic he from chush meaning hurry, translated here.
native_notes.71:15: Hebrew plays on the root sfr between yesapper, Piel meaning will recount, and the rare plural noun seforot meaning numbers or counts.
native_notes.71:20: Twice in this verse ketiv writes first-person plural suffixes, shown us and restore us to life, while qere reads first-person singular, shown me and restore me to life, matching the final singular verb bring me up and translated here.
native_notes.72:5: Masoretic Hebrew reads yir'uka (Qal imperfect of yare', "may they fear You"), addressing God directly, with the literal temporal idioms "with the sun" and "before the moon" expressing perpetual duration. Some ancient versions such as the Septuagint instead reflect a different verb meaning "may he endure."
native_notes.72:15: The verbs "give," "pray," and "bless" are third-person masculine singular with an indefinite subject, idiomatically rendered as passive ("be given," "prayer be offered," "be blessed"); alternatively, the rescued needy person of verses 12-14 may be the subject.
native_notes.72:16: The noun pissah ("abundance") is a biblical hapax legomenon, usually linked to an Aramaic root meaning "spread out" or "expand," though some understand it as "a handful."
native_notes.72:17: Qere yinnon (Niphal imperfect of the rare root nun, cognate with nin "offspring") means "may his name continue" or "be perpetuated"; Ketiv ynyn (vocalized as Hiphil yanin) means "may his name increase" or "put forth shoots."
native_notes.73:2: Two Ketiv/Qere variants occur here: Qere natayu (Qal perfect plural of natah, "had turned aside") vs. Ketiv ntwy (singular passive participle), and Qere shuppeku (Pual perfect plural of shafak, literally "were poured out," i.e., "slipped") vs. Ketiv shfkh (feminine singular Pual shuppekah agreeing collectively with "my steps").
native_notes.73:4: The Masoretic Text reads lemotam ("at their death"), alongside two rare nouns: hartsubbot ("pangs" or "bonds") and 'ulam ("their body" or "strength"). The consonants can also be divided as lamo tam ("for them; sound [is their body]"), which departs from the Masoretic division.
native_notes.73:10: Qere yashuv (Qal imperfect of shuv, "return") is translated here; Ketiv yshyb represents the Hiphil yashiv ("he brings back"). The second clause literally reads "and waters of fullness are drained by them," an idiom whose sense is debated (either drinking deeply of prosperity or draining a full cup of bitterness).
native_notes.73:16: Qere hu' (masculine singular pronoun agreeing with masculine 'amal, "trouble") vs. Ketiv hy' (feminine singular hi', agreeing with feminine zo't, "this").
native_notes.73:20: Hebrew ba'ir is generally understood as a contracted Hiphil infinitive construct of 'ur (for beha'ir, "when You stir/arouse Yourself," parallel to "upon waking"), though the same consonantal and vocalized form can literally mean "in the city."
native_notes.74:5: The Hebrew syntax is terse: yivvada' (Niphal imperfect of yada', "it appeared/was recognized") is followed by kemevi' lema'lah ("like one lifting upward") with plural qardummot ("axes") in a thicket of trees.
native_notes.74:6: Qere we'attah ("and now") is translated here; Ketiv w't either reflects defective orthography for we'attah or reads we'et ("and a time"). Both kashshil ("hatchet") and kelappot ("hammers") are biblical hapax legomena.
native_notes.74:11: Qere heqeka ("Your bosom," i.e., the fold of a garment) is translated here; Ketiv hwqk reflects a rare variant spelling hoqeka. The closing imperative kalleh (Piel of kalah, "consume/destroy") forms a pregnant construction implying "draw Your right hand out from Your bosom and consume them."
native_notes.74:14: Hebrew le'am letsiyyim literally reads "to the people, the desert dwellers"; here 'am ("people") may denote either human desert inhabitants or, poetically, a host of wilderness creatures (compare Proverbs 30:25-26).
native_notes.74:19: Hebrew hayyat appears twice with wordplay: first with an archaic feminine absolute ending meaning "to the wild beast" (following the Masoretic accents), and second in construct with "Your afflicted ones" meaning "the life of" (or "the community of") Your afflicted ones.
native_notes.75:2: The Masoretic verb rendered "people recount" is an impersonal third-person plural Piel perfect of the verb meaning to tell or recount, literally "they recount Your marvelous works."
native_notes.75:6: The negative particle "do not" from the first clause extends poetically to the second clause. The final phrase is literally "with a defiant neck," though the word rendered "defiant" elsewhere serves as a noun meaning "insolence," allowing "speak insolence with outstretched neck."
native_notes.75:7: The final Hebrew word can be parsed either as a Hiphil infinitive of the verb meaning to raise up used substantively ("raising up"), echoing verses 5, 6, and 8, or as the plural noun "mountains" forming a construct phrase "wilderness of mountains" with the preceding word.
native_notes.75:9: The noun rendered "spiced mixture" denotes a blend of wine and aromatic spices; the two Qal imperfect verbs "drain out and drink" stand side by side without a conjunction for emphasis.
native_notes.76:4: "Fiery bolts of the bow" is literally "flames of the bow," a poetic metaphor for swift, flashing arrows.
native_notes.76:5: "More majestic than the mountains of prey" translates the Masoretic preposition comparatively; it may alternatively be taken spatially as "majestic from the mountains of prey," continuing the lion-den imagery of verse 3.
native_notes.76:6: "Were despoiled" translates a rare Hithpolel perfect of the verb meaning to plunder, displaying an Aramaizing initial prefix. "Found their hands" is a literal Hebrew idiom for being able to act or fight.
native_notes.76:11: "The remnant of furies You will gird on" renders the Masoretic Qal imperfect of the verb meaning to tie or gird around the waist, picturing God wearing remaining human rage like a belt or trophy, or binding it in restraint.
native_notes.76:13: The Qal imperfect verb rendered "cuts off" is normally used of harvesting or snipping off grape clusters, applied here metaphorically to cutting away the spirit of rulers.
native_notes.77:1: Ketiv reads "Jedithun"; Qere reads "Jeduthun," the name of a Levitical chief musician.
native_notes.77:3: The Niphal perfect verb rendered "was stretched out" normally means "was poured out" or "flowed," here used of a hand extended without ceasing in nightlong prayer.
native_notes.77:11: This verse is a noted Hebrew crux: the form rendered "my affliction" can alternatively be parsed as a Piel infinitive meaning "my appeal," and "the changing of" (Qal infinitive construct of the verb to change) has the same form as the construct plural noun "the years of."
native_notes.77:12: Ketiv reads a Hiphil imperfect ("I will recall" or "cause to be remembered"); Qere reads a Qal imperfect ("I will remember"). The divine name here is the shortened poetic form of the LORD's name.
native_notes.77:20: Ketiv reads the plural "Your paths"; Qere reads the singular "Your path."
native_notes.78:9: The Hebrew phrase uses two successive Qal construct participles (noshqei romei-qashet, literally "armed ones, shooters of the bow") to describe equipped archers.
native_notes.78:15: Hebrew pairs the plural noun tehomot ("depths") with the feminine singular adjective rabbah ("great" or "abundant"), functioning either as a poetic collective ("the great depths") or adverbially ("abundantly, like the depths").
native_notes.78:25: Literally "bread of mighty ones" (lechem abbirim), referring poetically to heavenly beings; the Septuagint interprets the phrase as "bread of angels."
native_notes.78:28: Hebrew uses masculine singular possessive suffixes (literally "its/his camp" and "its/his dwellings") despite plural pronouns in verses 27 and 29; the singular refers collectively to Israel, though some read it as referring to God.
native_notes.78:41: The rare Hiphil verb hitwu is commonly derived from a cognate root meaning "to cause pain" or "provoke," paralleling "grieved Him" in verse 40; others connect it to Hebrew tawah ("to mark") and render "set limits on."
native_notes.78:47: The Hebrew word chanamal occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; ancient versions and the parallel with "hail" support translating it as "frost" or "sleet."
native_notes.78:63: The Pual verb hullalu literally means "were praised," referring idiomatically to bridal wedding songs; here and in verse 64, the Hebrew masculine singular possessive suffixes refer collectively to "His people" in verse 62.
native_notes.78:69: Hebrew kemo-ramim literally means "like the heights" (referring to the lofty heavens), whereas the Septuagint translates a similar-looking word meaning "wild oxen."
native_notes.79:2: The phrase rendered beasts of the earth uses the archaic poetic construct ending -o on chayto (chayto-arets), literally "living creature of the earth," employed collectively for wild animals.
native_notes.79:7: The Masoretic Text has the collective third-person masculine singular Qal perfect verb akhal (literally "he has devoured") before shifting to the third-person plural Hiphil heshammu ("they have made desolate").
native_notes.79:8: The phrase avonot rishonim can be read either attributively as "former iniquities" (since avon is grammatically masculine despite its -ot plural ending) or as a construct chain meaning "iniquities of ancestors."
native_notes.79:11: Hebrew hoter is a Hiphil imperative of yatar ("cause to remain," hence "spare"), and bene temutah is literally "sons of death," an idiom for people condemned to die.
native_notes.80:5: As elsewhere in the Elohistic Psalter (see also 79:8, 15, 20), Elohim stands in the absolute state rather than construct Elohei before Tsevaot ("hosts"). The Qal perfect verb ashanta literally means "you have smoked" or "fumed," a metaphor for smoldering anger.
native_notes.80:6: Hebrew shalish literally denotes "a third" (a substantial dry or liquid measure, cf. Isa 40:12), used metaphorically here for tears poured out in large measure.
native_notes.80:11: The phrase arzei-el (literally "cedars of God") is a Hebrew idiom for towering, mighty cedars; the Pual perfect verb kossu ("were covered") from the first clause carries over chiastically into the second.
native_notes.80:14: The quadriliteral verb yekharsemennah (from krsm) is a biblical hapax legomenon meaning to gnaw off or strip bare, and ziz sadai is a poetic phrase for wild moving creatures of the open field.
native_notes.80:16: Hebrew kannah is a hapax legomenon usually taken as a noun meaning "stock" or "rootstock" (related to ken, "base"), though some parse it as a Qal imperative meaning "protect"; the Masoretic Text reads simply ben ("son") rather than "son of man" as in 79:18.
native_notes.81:1: The musical or liturgical term ha-gittit ("the Gittith") is uncertain in origin, possibly denoting a melody or instrument linked to Gath or to winepresses (gat).
native_notes.81:6: The name Joseph is spelled uniquely here as Yehosef. The suffix on be-tseto ("when he/He went out") is ambiguous and can refer either to God marching out against Egypt at the Exodus (cf. Exod 11:4) or to Joseph going out over Egypt (cf. Gen 41:45).
native_notes.81:16: The Piel verb yekhachashu with le- literally means to act deceptively toward someone, hence to feign obedience or offer reluctant submission; Hebrew ittam is literally "their time," leaving open whether it denotes the enemies' lasting doom or Israel's enduring era.
native_notes.81:17: The Masoretic Text has the third-person masculine singular Hiphil verb and suffix wayya'akhilehu ("and He would feed him") before shifting back to first- and second-person singular in asbi'ekha ("I would satisfy you"), a poetic person shift characteristic of prophetic speech; "choicest wheat" is literally "fat of wheat" (chelev chittah).
native_notes.82:1: Hebrew ba'adat-'el ("in the assembly of God") can also be rendered "in the divine assembly"; the second 'elohim ("gods") refers to heavenly beings or human judges summoned before God.
native_notes.82:2: Hebrew "lift up the faces of the wicked" (tise'u ... pene resha'im) is an idiom for showing judicial partiality; "Selah" is a liturgical or musical direction of uncertain meaning.
native_notes.82:7: Hebrew ke'adam can be understood collectively as "like mortals" or as a proper name, "like Adam."
native_notes.83:4: Hebrew tsefunekha ("Your sheltered ones") is the Qal passive participle of tsafan ("hide, treasure, shelter"), referring to God's protected people.
native_notes.83:9: Hebrew "an arm" (zeroa') is a metaphor for military strength and active support.
native_notes.83:14: Hebrew galgal literally means "wheel" or "whirling thing," here referring to windblown tumbleweed or swirling dry plant debris.
native_notes.83:19: Hebrew places shimkha followed by the divine name ("Your name is the LORD") in emphatic apposition between 'attah ("You") and levaddekha ("alone").
native_notes.84:4: The preposition 'et before "Your altars" is understood here as "beside" or "at," though some take it as an exclamatory object marker.
native_notes.84:6: Hebrew mesillot bilvavam ("highways are in their heart") refers to the pilgrimage roads leading to Zion and shifts from collective singular 'adam ("person") to a plural pronominal suffix.
native_notes.84:7: Baca may denote a balsam shrub or evoke "weeping"; the Masoretic pointing reads berakhot ("blessings") rather than berekhot ("pools"), and moreh here denotes the autumn early rain.
native_notes.84:10: Hebrew maginnenu ("our shield") may be read either as the direct object of re'eh ("look upon"), in parallel with "Your anointed" (the king), or as a vocative title for God (cf. v. 12).
native_notes.84:11: Hebrew histofef is a Hithpoel infinitive construct formed from saf ("threshold"), occurring only here, and dur ("lodge, dwell") is attested in this sense only here in Biblical Hebrew.
native_notes.85:2: Ketiv reads shvut ("fortunes" or "captivity"), while the Qere followed here reads shevit ("captivity," derived from shabah, "take captive").
native_notes.85:5: The verb shubenu is a Qal imperative of shuv ("turn, return") with an object suffix used transitively to mean "restore us," continuing the psalm's recurring shuv motif (vv. 2, 4, 5, 7, 9).
native_notes.85:14: The terse second clause literally reads "and will make His steps for a path," personifying righteousness as a herald going ahead of the LORD and turning His footsteps into a way to follow.
native_notes.86:5: The adjective sallach ("forgiving") uses an intensive pattern from salach ("forgive") and appears only here in the Hebrew Bible, denoting an abiding disposition to forgive.
native_notes.86:11: The verb yached ("unify") is a Piel imperative of yachad ("be one, unite"), asking for an undivided heart, whereas the Septuagint reads a form of chadah ("rejoice").
native_notes.86:13: Literally "lowest Sheol," using the feminine adjective tachtiyyah with feminine Sheol to denote the deepest realm of the dead.
native_notes.86:17: Literally "perform with me a sign for good," reflecting the Hebrew idiom asah im ("act on behalf of, deal with").
native_notes.87:1: The noun yesudato ("His foundation") occurs only here and bears a masculine singular suffix referring to the LORD (since Zion and "city" are feminine in vv. 3, 5, 7), pointing to the city He founded on the plural "holy mountains."
native_notes.87:3: Literally "glorious things, it is spoken concerning you," combining a fronted feminine plural Niphal participle (nichbadot) with an impersonal masculine singular Pual participle (medubbar).
native_notes.87:4: "Rahab" is a poetic name for Egypt (compare Isa 30:7), listed with Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Cush as former rival nations enrolled among those who know God.
native_notes.87:5: "Each and every one" translates the distributive idiom ish ve-ish (literally "man and man"), paired with the singular passive verb yullad ("was born").
native_notes.87:7: The Hebrew clause is verbless ("will say" is implied), and the participle cholelim may mean either "dancers" (from chul, "whirl, dance") or "flute players" (denominative from chalil, "flute").
native_notes.88:1: Mahalath Leannoth transliterates Hebrew machalat leannot, a musical or liturgical heading of uncertain sense (possibly a tune title or direction meaning "for singing responsively" or "concerning affliction"); Maskil transliterates maskil (Hiphil participle of skl), a psalm genre term often taken as a contemplative or skillful poem.
native_notes.88:6: Hebrew chophshi ("turned loose") normally denotes a freed slave released from service, used here ironically of being cut loose among the dead beyond God's active care.
native_notes.88:8: The Hebrew clause omits both "with" and "me," literally reading "and all Your breakers You have afflicted" (Piel perfect of anah II), understood instrumentally as "with all Your breakers You have afflicted me."
native_notes.88:16: Hebrew aphunah ("I am numb") is a biblical hapax legomenon, usually parsed as a cohortative Qal imperfect of pun with an uncertain meaning variously rendered "numb," "helpless," or "at a loss."
native_notes.88:19: Hebrew meyudda'ay machshak is a stark verbless clause literally reading "my acquaintances, darkness," conveying either that darkness is the psalmist's only remaining company or that his acquaintances have vanished into darkness.
native_notes.89:7: Hebrew bene elim ("divine beings") literally means "sons of gods" or "sons of mighty ones," a poetic idiom for members of God's heavenly council (parallel to "the holy ones" in 88:6, 8).
native_notes.89:18: The qere tarum (Qal imperfect 3fs, "our horn is lifted high") is translated here; the ketiv reads a Hiphil imperfect 2ms ("You lift high our horn").
native_notes.89:23: Hebrew yashi with the preposition be (nasha I, Hiphil) denotes a creditor making exactions ("exact tribute from him"), though some derive it from nasha II ("deceive" or "outwit").
native_notes.89:29: The ketiv and qere differ only orthographically (plene versus defective spelling before maqqef); both are the Qal imperfect 1cs of shamar ("I will keep").
native_notes.89:45: Hebrew mitteharo ("his luster") is a difficult form, parsed either as the preposition min plus tohar ("luster, brightness, purity") or as a rare prefixed noun from the same root.
native_notes.89:51: The Hebrew clause is compressed and unusual in word order, literally reading "my bearing in my bosom all many peoples," carrying over "taunt" from the first half of the verse by ellipsis.
native_notes.90:2: MT vocalizes the verb as Polel 2ms active ("You brought ... to birth") from the root chul (to writhe in labor or give birth), taking "earth and world" as its direct object; some ancient versions reflect a passive reading ("were brought forth").
native_notes.90:5: The Qal verb chalaph ("grows anew") here and in 89:6 can mean either "sprout anew / renew itself" or "pass away"; the morning-versus-evening contrast in 89:6 supports the sense of fresh growth.
native_notes.90:10: The Hebrew noun rohab ("boast" or "pride") occurs only here in the Old Testament and denotes what is proudest or best in a human lifespan.
native_notes.90:11: The second clause is concise in Hebrew and may be read either as a second object of "Who knows" or as an independent statement: "as the fear due You is, so is Your wrath."
native_notes.91:2: MT reads Qal imperfect 1cs ("I say"), whereas the Septuagint reflects a participle ("saying") linking smoothly to the third-person subject of 90:1.
native_notes.91:4: The noun socherah ("rampart") is a Hebrew hapax legomenon derived from the root sachar ("to surround"), signifying a protective surrounding wall or buckler.
native_notes.91:9: Following the Masoretic accentuation, the verse shifts from the psalmist's first-person confession ("For You, LORD, are my refuge") to second-person reassurance ("you have made the Most High your dwelling place"); some alternatively take the first "you" as the believer, reading "Because you have made the LORD, my refuge, the Most High, your dwelling place."
native_notes.91:14: God speaks in the first person in 90:14-16; the Piel verb sagab ("set high in safety") carries the spatial image of lifting someone onto an inaccessible height beyond reach of harm.
native_notes.92:4: The noun higgayon ("resonant melody") comes from the root hagah ("murmur, resound, meditate") and here denotes solemn or resonant instrumental sound on the lyre.
native_notes.92:11: MT vocalizes balloti as Qal perfect 1cs of balal ("mix, pour over, moisten"), yielding an intransitive or passive sense ("I have been drenched"); an emendation to 2ms would yield "You have poured over me."
native_notes.92:16: The qere reads awlatah (plene spelling with medial vav, a poetic feminine form of awlah, "injustice/unrighteousness"), whereas the ketiv writes the same word defectively without the vav.
native_notes.93:3: The Hebrew noun translated "crashing waves" (dokyam) is a hapax legomenon from the root dkh ("pound, crush"), literally "their pounding." The shift from two Qal perfect verbs ("have lifted up") to an imperfect verb ("lift up") underscores the ongoing roar of the rivers.
native_notes.93:4: The Masoretic Hebrew places the plural adjective addirim ("mighty") directly before "breakers of the sea" without repeating the comparative preposition min ("above/more than") from the opening phrase. Translating the middle clause parenthetically preserves the unemended Masoretic syntax and the repeated root addir ("mighty").
native_notes.93:5: "For length of days" renders the Hebrew idiom le-orek yamim literally, expressing unending duration.
native_notes.94:4: "Boast" renders the rare Hithpael of amar ("speak"), used reflexively here in the sense of vaunting or talking arrogantly of oneself.
native_notes.94:7: Here (and in v. 12) the Hebrew uses Yah, the poetic shortened form of the divine name, rendered "the LORD."
native_notes.94:10: The final participial clause ("the One who teaches mankind knowledge") has no explicit interrogative predicate in the Hebrew, functioning either in apposition to the opening subject or as an elliptical question answered immediately in v. 11.
native_notes.94:17: "Silence" (dumah) is a poetic Hebrew designation for the grave or the realm of the dead.
native_notes.94:20: "Be joined with You" renders an unusually vocalized form of chabar ("be allied, joined"), and the phrase aley-choq ("by statute") can mean either "under the cover of a legal decree" or "contrary to statute."
native_notes.95:4: "Deep recesses" translates the hapax legomenon mechqerey (from chaqar, "search out, fathom"), and "summits" translates the rare plural toafot, whose exact etymology is debated but whose meaning "heights/peaks" is clear from the merism with the earth's depths.
native_notes.95:7: The clause "if only you would listen to His voice" reflects the Hebrew optative use of im ("if") without a stated consequence, expressing an urgent wish that introduces God's direct words in vv. 8-11.
native_notes.95:8: The place names Meribah ("Quarreling") and Massah ("Testing") recall Israel's rebellion in the wilderness (Exod 17:7; Num 20:13), with Massah echoed by the verb "tested" (nissuni, from nasah) in v. 9.
native_notes.95:10: The Hebrew literally reads "with a generation" (bedor) without a definite article or demonstrative, understood contextually in Hebrew poetry as "that generation."
native_notes.95:11: "They will certainly not come" renders the emphatic Hebrew negative oath formula im followed by an imperfect verb with paragogic nun (yevo'un), literally "if they enter."
native_notes.96:5: The Hebrew pairs elohim ("gods") with elilim ("empty idols"), a wordplay contrasting the living God with false deities characterized as worthless or nothing.
native_notes.96:9: The construct phrase hadrat-qodesh ("the splendor of holiness") uses a noun from the same root as "splendor" in 95:6 and can refer either to the LORD's own holy majesty or to the sacred attire worn by worshipers.
native_notes.96:13: The form ba ("is coming") is identical in vocalization for both the Qal perfect and the Qal participle of bo, expressing the LORD's imminent arrival; the doubled ki ba emphasizes certainty.
native_notes.97:1: The Hebrew noun iyyim ("coastlands") denotes not only islands but also distant coastal lands and maritime regions.
native_notes.97:7: The Hishtaphel form hishtachavu ("bow down") is identical for both the second-person plural imperative ("bow down to Him, all you gods") and the third-person plural perfect ("all gods have bowed down to Him"); context and early witnesses favor the imperative.
native_notes.97:8: "The daughters of Judah" may denote the towns and villages of Judah (a Hebrew idiom for dependent settlements) or the women of Judah.
native_notes.97:11: The Masoretic Text reads the Qal passive participle zarua ("has been sown"), portraying light as seed planted for the righteous, whereas some ancient versions read the similar verb zarach ("dawns" or "shines").
native_notes.97:12: Literally "to the remembrance of His holiness," where zeker ("remembrance" or "memorial") denotes the name and renown by which the LORD is remembered and invoked.
native_notes.98:1: The Hiphil perfect verb hoshiah ("has brought salvation") is feminine singular, agreeing grammatically with the nearest subject, "His right hand" (feminine in Hebrew), and shares the same root as "salvation" in 97:2-3.
native_notes.98:4: The Hiphil imperative hariu ("shout in triumph," repeated in 97:6) denotes a loud cry of victory or royal acclamation, often accompanied by horn blasts.
native_notes.98:6: Hebrew distinguishes two instruments here: the chatsotserot ("trumpets," straight metal instruments used by priests) and the shofar ("ram's horn").
native_notes.99:1: The verb translated 'reels' (Hebrew tanut, Qal imperfect of nut) is a hapax legomenon in the Hebrew Bible meaning to totter, sway, or reel. Both imperfect verbs in this verse ('tremble' and 'reels') may also be read as jussives ('let the peoples tremble ... let the earth reel').
native_notes.99:4: Hebrew oz melekh is literally 'the might of a king' (a construct phrase expressing 'the mighty King') serving as the grammatical subject of the verb 'loves.'
native_notes.99:8: Hebrew el nose uses the Qal active participle of nasa ('lift, bear'), an idiom for bearing away or forgiving guilt. Hebrew alilotam literally means 'their deeds' or 'their practices,' referring in context to their sinful actions.
native_notes.100:1: Hebrew letodah can mean either 'for thanksgiving' or 'for a thank offering' (compare Lev 7:12). The imperative hari'u (Hiphil of rua) denotes raising a loud shout of acclamation or joy.
native_notes.100:3: The translation follows the qere (read text) velo ('and to Him,' i.e., 'and we belong to Him'). The ketiv (written text) reads velo spelled with aleph ('and not'), yielding 'and not we ourselves.'
native_notes.101:2: Hebrew askilah (Hiphil cohortative of sakhal) with the preposition be- can mean either 'I will give attention to' (ponder with insight) or 'I will act wisely in' the blameless way.
native_notes.101:3: Hebrew asoh-setim pairs the Qal infinitive construct of asah ('do, practice') with the rare plural noun setim (from sut, 'swerve, turn aside'), meaning either 'the practice of unfaithful deeds' or 'the work of those who turn aside.'
native_notes.101:5: Ketiv and qere differ only in spelling: the ketiv writes meloshni plene with a vav, while the qere writes it defectively with qamets hatuf; both are participles of lashan ('slander') with the archaic poetic ending -i (hireq compaginis). Hebrew rehav levav ('an arrogant heart') is literally 'broad of heart,' an idiom for swollen pride.
native_notes.101:8: Hebrew labbeqarim ('morning by morning') is a distributive plural meaning 'every morning,' reflecting the ancient practice of administering royal justice each morning.
native_notes.102:7: The Hebrew bird names קָאַת (possibly a pelican or a desert owl) and כּוֹס (little owl) designate unclean birds associated with desolate places, and their exact ornithological identification remains uncertain.
native_notes.102:9: The participle מְהוֹלָלַי (Poal of הלל) literally refers to those maddened or raging against the speaker, while בִּי נִשְׁבָּעוּ (literally, swear by me) is an idiom for using someone's misery as a curse formula.
native_notes.102:21: Literally, sons of death (בְּנֵי תְמוּתָה), a Hebrew idiom denoting people sentenced or doomed to die.
native_notes.102:24: Ketiv reads כחו (his strength), whereas Qere reads כֹּחִי (my strength); the translation follows Qere, matching the first-person my days in the parallel clause.
native_notes.102:27: The verse uses a wordplay on the root חלף, shifting from the Hiphil תַּחֲלִיפֵם (You will replace or change them) to the Qal וְיַחֲלֹפוּ (and they will pass away).
native_notes.103:3: Verses 3 through 5 employ the poetic second-person feminine singular pronominal suffix -î (as in עֲוֺנֵכִי and תַּחֲלוּאָיְכִי), addressing the psalmist's feminine soul (נַפְשִׁי).
native_notes.103:5: The noun עֶדְיֵךְ is lexically difficult; it normally means ornament or finery, but in parallel with your youth it is widely understood as lifetime or existence.
native_notes.103:9: The Qal verb יִטּוֹר (from נטר, keep or guard) is used absolutely in Hebrew as an idiom for retaining anger or holding a grudge.
native_notes.103:14: The noun יִצְרֵנוּ (our form, from יצר, to form) recalls humanity's shaping from dust, and זָכוּר is a Qal passive participle of זכר used statively with an active sense, mindful.
native_notes.104:4: The double accusative after the Qal participle of asah ('make') can be construed either as 'making winds His messengers, blazing fire His attendants' (fitting the meteorological imagery of v. 3) or following the Hebrew word order as 'making His messengers winds [or spirits], His attendants a blazing fire' (the construal reflected in the Septuagint).
native_notes.104:8: The masculine plural Qal imperfects 'went up' and 'descended' continue the grammatical subject 'waters' from vv. 6-7 and match the masculine plural references in vv. 8b-9; alternatively, 'mountains' and 'valleys' may be construed as their subjects ('the mountains rose, the valleys sank down').
native_notes.104:13: The Masoretic Hebrew shifts abruptly within this verse from third person ('His upper chambers') to second person ('Your works'), a frequent feature of hymnic praise in this psalm.
native_notes.104:26: The Hebrew prepositional phrase 'bo' after the Piel infinitive of sachaq ('play, sport') can refer either to the sea ('to play in it') or to Leviathan with God as subject ('for You to play with it'; cf. Job 41:5).
native_notes.104:29: The verb tosef ('withdraw') is the Qal imperfect of asaf ('gather in, withdraw') with elided initial aleph (cf. Job 34:14), not Hiphil of yasaf ('add'); the noun ruach ('breath') here echoes 'Your Spirit' (also ruach, or 'Your breath') in v. 30.
native_notes.105:18: The Masoretic read form (qere) is singular ("his foot"), whereas the written form (ketiv) is plural ("his feet"). In the second clause, the feminine Qal perfect verb ("came") takes the feminine noun "his soul" (meaning his person or neck) as its subject, with "iron" as the adverbial accusative of goal.
native_notes.105:22: The Masoretic Hebrew reads the Qal infinitive "to bind" (rather than "to instruct"), reflecting Joseph's authority over Pharaoh's officials; "at his will" translates the idiom "by his soul/desire."
native_notes.105:28: The qere (read form) is singular ("His word"), while the ketiv (written form) is plural ("His words"). The Masoretic text explicitly includes the negative particle ("and they did not rebel"), referring either to Moses and Aaron carrying out God's commands or to the plagues obeying His word.
native_notes.105:40: The Hebrew Qal perfect verb "asked" is grammatically singular, functioning collectively for the people of Israel (rendered "They asked" to agree with the plural pronoun "them" in the second clause).
native_notes.106:20: The Masoretic Text reads "their glory," referring to God as Israel's glory. Ancient Jewish scribal tradition lists this among the Tiqqune Soferim, where an earlier reading "My glory" or "His glory" was discussed.
native_notes.106:26: "Lifted His hand" is a Biblical Hebrew idiom for swearing a solemn oath (cf. Num 14:30; Ezek 20:23). In v. 27, the Masoretic Text repeats the Hiphil infinitive of npl ("to cause to fall") rather than "to scatter" as in the parallel Ezekiel 20:23.
native_notes.106:30: The verb translated "executed judgment" is the Piel of pll, meaning to intervene, arbitrate, or execute judgment (distinct from the Hithpael, "to pray"), fitting Phinehas's decisive action in Numbers 25:7-8.
native_notes.106:33: The verb translated "rebelled against" is the Hiphil of mrh (as in vv. 7 and 43). Because Moses is named in v. 32 and is the subject of the next clause, "His Spirit" may alternatively be understood as "his spirit" (Moses's spirit), taking the verb in the sense of provoking or embittering him.
native_notes.106:45: The Hebrew form for "His acts of loyal love" is written defectively without a yod (resembling the singular Ketiv) but vocalized as plural, matching the plural Qere tradition and v. 7. The verb "relented" is the Niphal of nhm, expressing God's turning from judgment in compassion.
native_notes.107:3: Hebrew miyyam literally means "from the sea," which normally denotes the west; because "from the west" has already been named, it stands here in the fourth compass position, often understood as the southern sea or the south.
native_notes.107:4: Following the Masoretic accentuation with pausal derek ("path"), "on a wasteland path" closes the first half-verse and contrasts with "along a straight path" in v. 7; some instead construe derek with the second clause as "no way to a city to live in."
native_notes.107:10: Hebrew tsalmavet is pointed by the Masoretes as a compound meaning "shadow of death," though many lexicographers derive it from a root meaning "be dark" and take it as "deep shadow" or "utter gloom."
native_notes.107:25: The masculine singular suffix on gallaw ("its waves") refers back to the masculine noun "the sea" in v. 23, while the plural suffix on gallehem ("their waves") in v. 29 refers to the waves of the "mighty waters" of v. 23 or the waves threatening the sailors.
native_notes.107:27: Hebrew titballa is the Hithpael of bala ("swallow"), literally "was swallowed up," an idiom conveying that all their seamanship and skill vanished completely.
native_notes.108:2: Hebrew af-kevodi ("even [with] my glory") uses "my glory" as a poetic idiom for one's inner self or soul, functioning adverbially or appositionally with the preceding cohortatives.
native_notes.108:8: Hebrew be-qodsho can mean either "in His holiness" or "in His sanctuary."
native_notes.108:9: Hebrew mehoqeqi is the Poel active participle of haqaq ("inscribe, decree") with a first-person suffix, denoting either a commander's scepter ("My ruler's staff") or "My lawgiver."
native_notes.108:10: Hebrew etroa is the first-person Hithpolel imperfect of rua ("shout in triumph"), continuing God's direct speech over Philistia.
native_notes.109:4: The verbless clause translated "while I am at prayer" is literally "and I am prayer," expressing complete absorption in prayer. The verb "accuse" shares the root satan with "accuser" in v. 6 and "accusers" in vv. 20 and 29.
native_notes.109:10: The verb pair noa yanuu combines a Qal infinitive absolute with the imperfect for emphasis ("constantly wander about"), followed by the Piel of shaal ("beg"). The final clause follows the Masoretic reading darshu ("search") rather than the Septuagint's "be driven out."
native_notes.109:21: The reversed divine title, the divine name followed by Adonai ("GOD the Lord"), points the divine name with the vowels of Elohim to avoid reading Adonai twice. The imperative phrase aseh itti (literally "do with me") is an elliptical idiom meaning "act favorably on my behalf."
native_notes.109:23: The verb nehelakhti is the sole Niphal occurrence of halakh ("go") in the Hebrew Bible, conveying being swept or carried away like a lengthening evening shadow.
native_notes.110:1: The construct noun neum ("declaration" or "oracle") introduces a formal prophetic utterance. The Masoretic pointing laadoni ("to my lord") is the form normally used in addressing a human superior, in contrast to the divine title Adonai ("the Lord") in v. 5.
native_notes.110:3: This verse translates the dense Masoretic Hebrew directly: nedavot ("freewill offerings") depicts eager voluntary service, behadrei-qodesh means "in splendors of holiness," and "the dew of your youth" evokes fresh royal vigor or youthful warriors.
native_notes.110:4: The phrase al-divrati preserves an archaic connective -i ending on divrah ("manner" or "order"), literally "according to the manner of Melchizedek."
native_notes.110:7: Grammatically, the third-person subject continues from "the Lord" in v. 5, though many interpreters understand v. 7 as shifting back to the victorious king refreshing himself along the campaign route.
native_notes.111:1: Following the opening "Praise the LORD," this psalm is a 22-line alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew, with each successive poetic line beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet from alef to tav.
native_notes.111:2: The Qal passive participle derushim ("sought out") is followed by lekhol-cheftseihem ("by all who take delight in them"), with the plural suffix referring back to the LORD's works.
native_notes.111:10: The plural pronoun in "all who practice them" (oseihem) translates the Masoretic suffix literally, referring back to the LORD's precepts in vv. 7-8.
native_notes.112:1: After the opening call "Praise the LORD" (Hebrew halelu-Yah, using the poetic shortened divine name), this psalm is an alphabetic acrostic whose twenty-two poetic lines begin with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet.
native_notes.112:4: The three masculine singular adjectives "gracious, compassionate, and righteous" have no explicit subject in Hebrew; in context they describe the God-fearing man of vv. 1-9 (echoing "gracious" in v. 5 and "righteous" in v. 6), though some interpreters take the LORD as the implied subject.
native_notes.112:8: The Hebrew idiom "look on" (ra'ah with the preposition be-) used with foes conveys looking in triumph or vindication upon their defeat.
native_notes.113:5: Verses 5-9 contain five verb forms with the archaic poetic ending -i (hireq compaginis) attached to four participles and one infinitive construct. The paired Hiphil participles in vv. 5-6 literally contrast making high to sit with making low to look.
native_notes.113:9: Literally "the barren woman of the house," a construct phrase referring to a childless woman within a household; the Hiphil participle of yashav ("settle / cause to dwell") echoes the same root in v. 5 ("sits") and v. 8 ("seat").
native_notes.114:1: The Qal active participle lo'ez ("speaking a foreign language") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes speech unintelligible to Israel.
native_notes.114:8: Both halves of this verse employ archaic poetic linking endings: hireq compaginis (-i) on the Qal participle "who transforms" and holem compaginis (-o) on the construct noun "wellspring of."
native_notes.115:7: Whereas vv. 13-14 state literally "a mouth/eyes/ears/nose they have," v. 15 shifts to possessive suffixes ("their hands," "their feet") standing in casus pendens before masculine plural verbs whose subject remains the idols themselves. Both "touch" here and "smell" in v. 14 carry the archaic paragogic nun ending (-un).
native_notes.115:9: Here and in vv. 18-19, the Hebrew shifts from a second-person imperative ("trust") to third-person suffixes ("their helper and their shield"), reflecting an antiphonal liturgical call and response. The noun ezer literally means "help" and is used concretely of God as helper.
native_notes.116:1: Hebrew has no explicit direct object after the verb 'I love,' taking the following clause either as its content ('that the LORD hears') or causally with an implied object ('I love Him, because the LORD hears').
native_notes.116:3: The verse pairs repeated Hebrew roots for poetic effect: 'straits' and 'distress' share the root meaning narrowness or confinement, and the verb 'found' (Qal of matsa) recurs in both halves.
native_notes.116:6: The verb 'saved' (yehoshia) is an unusual uncontracted Hiphil imperfect of yasha that retains the characteristic he prefix; 'I sank low' renders the stative Qal of dalal ('become low or depleted').
native_notes.116:7: Both 'your rest' (plural of abstraction) and 'with you' display the poetic, Aramaic-influenced feminine singular suffix -ayki addressing the psalmist's soul.
native_notes.116:9: The verb 'walk about' renders the Hithpael of halak, conveying continual or free movement, and the Hebrew noun 'lands' (artsot) is plural rather than singular.
native_notes.116:10: The syntax of the clause ki adabber is debated: taking ki as temporal-concessive ('even as I spoke') introduces the lament that follows, whereas ancient versions such as the Septuagint read ki as consequential ('therefore I spoke').
native_notes.116:12: 'His generous deeds' renders a unique Hebrew noun (tagmulohi) from the same root as 'dealt generously' in 114:7, bearing an Aramaic-style masculine singular possessive suffix (-ohi).
native_notes.116:15: 'Costly' (yaqar, literally 'precious' or 'weighty') expresses that the LORD does not treat the death of His loyal ones lightly; the noun 'death' (hammavtah) carries a poetic -ah ending.
native_notes.116:16: 'Untied' renders the Piel of patach with the preposition le marking the direct object ('my bonds'), an Aramaic-influenced construction.
native_notes.116:19: 'Within you' (betokeki) uses an Aramaic-influenced feminine singular suffix addressing Jerusalem, and 'Praise the LORD!' renders the liturgical call halelu-yah ('Praise Yah,' a shortened poetic form of the LORD's name).
native_notes.117:1: 'Acclaim Him' translates the Piel imperative of shabach, a poetic synonym for praise prominent in Aramaic, and Hebrew uses the definite article with 'the peoples' in contrast to anarthrous 'nations.'
native_notes.117:2: 'Has prevailed' translates the Qal perfect of gabar ('be mighty' or 'prevail'), and the second clause is verbless in Hebrew, literally 'and the faithfulness of the LORD forever.'
native_notes.118:5: Hebrew uses the shortened poetic divine name Yah here and in vv. 14 and 17-19. The clause anani bammerchav is a pregnant construction, literally "answered me in the open expanse," contrasting directly with hammetsar, "the narrow straits/distress."
native_notes.118:12: The Masoretic Text reads the Pual verb do'akhu ("they were extinguished/snuffed out"), rather than the Septuagint's "they blazed up." In vv. 10-12, amilam is a Hiphil imperfect of mul ("cut off") reinforced by emphatic ki ("certainly").
native_notes.118:13: The Masoretic Text has the Qal infinitive absolute with a 2ms Qal perfect of dachah (dachoh dechitani, literally "pushing you pushed me"), addressing the adversary directly rather than the passive "I was pushed" of several ancient versions.
native_notes.118:16: Romemah is a rare feminine singular form from rum ("be high"), matching the feminine subject yemin ("right hand"); it is taken here intransitively ("is raised high"), though some parse it as an active Polel participle lacking the m- prefix ("exalts").
native_notes.118:27: The command isru-chag ba'avotim ad-qarnot hammizbeach is famously difficult; it is rendered literally here taking chag by metonymy for the festival sacrifice (cf. Exod 23:18; Mal 2:3) and avotim as "ropes/cords," though others understand it as "join the festival procession with leafy branches up to the horns of the altar."
native_notes.119:20: The verb translated 'is broken' is a Qal perfect of garas, literally 'be crushed' or 'ground down,' and the noun translated 'longing' occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, cognate with the verb 'longed' in 118:40.
native_notes.119:22: The imperative gal is commonly parsed as a Qal of galal, meaning 'roll away' and matching the idiom with 'reproach' in Joshua 5:9, though some take it as an apocopated Piel of galah, meaning 'remove' or 'uncover' as in 118:18.
native_notes.119:33: The Hebrew noun eqev, literally 'heel,' is used adverbially here to mean 'to the end,' though some interpreters take it in its related sense 'as a reward.'
native_notes.119:38: Literally 'which is for the fear of You'; this terse relative clause may describe God's spoken word as leading to the fear of Him, or alternatively modify 'Your servant' as one devoted to fearing Him.
native_notes.119:49: The Piel of yahal ('wait, hope') takes a personal object suffix only here in the Hebrew Bible, functioning causatively: 'You have caused me to hope.'
native_notes.119:61: The Piel verb translated 'have surrounded' (from the root 'ud) occurs in this sense of winding around or encircling only here in the Hebrew Bible.
native_notes.119:70: The verb translated 'has grown thick' (tafash) occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes being thick, gross, or insensitive.
native_notes.119:79: Translated according to the Masoretic Qere (read text), 'and those who know' (a plural construct participle); the Ketiv (written text) reads a finite verb, 'and may they know' or 'that they may know.'
native_notes.119:96: The noun tikhlah ('perfection' or 'completeness') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, formed from the root kalah ('be complete, come to an end').
native_notes.119:103: The Niphal verb nimletsu ('are sweet' or 'pleasant') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, and the noun rendered 'palate' refers literally to the roof of the mouth as the seat of taste.
native_notes.119:113: The plural noun se'afim ('the double-minded' or 'divided ones') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, related to the noun for 'divided opinions' in 1 Kings 18:21.
native_notes.119:128: The Masoretic Text reads literally 'all precepts of all' (meaning all precepts concerning everything), with the estimative Piel yisharti ('I regard as right'); some ancient versions read 'all Your precepts.'
native_notes.119:147: Translated according to the Masoretic Qere (read text), singular 'Your word'; the Ketiv (written text) is plural, 'Your words.'
native_notes.119:160: The noun rosh (literally 'head') here carries the sense of 'sum' or 'entirety' (as in Exodus 30:12), though some understand it as 'beginning.'
native_notes.119:161: Translated according to the Masoretic Qere (read text), singular 'Your word'; the Ketiv (written text) is plural, 'Your words.'
native_notes.119:175: The noun mishpatekha ('Your judgments') is written defectively without yod, as in 118:43 and 118:149, yet the plural verb ya'zeruni ('help me') confirms its plural meaning.
native_notes.120:3: The third-person masculine singular verbs (Qal yitten, "give," and Hiphil yosif, "add") have no explicit subject, referring either to the LORD from verse 2 (echoing the Hebrew oath formula) or to an indefinite subject, "What will be given to you, and what will be added to you."
native_notes.120:5: Meshech (in northern Asia Minor) and Kedar (an Arabian nomadic tribe) represent distant, hostile regions; Hebrew uses the unique form oyah (for oy, "woe") and the Qal verb gur ("sojourn as a resident alien").
native_notes.120:7: Hebrew reads literally "I am peace" (a verbless nominal clause without a preposition), contrasting sharply with the final clause, literally "they are for the war."
native_notes.121:1: Unlike the other Songs of the Ascents (which use the construct phrase "song of the ascents"), this superscription uses the preposition le- ("for the ascents").
native_notes.121:3: Hebrew uses the jussive negative particle al ("may ... not") in both clauses of verse 3 before shifting to the indicative negative lo ("not") in verse 4, though poetic al can also express emphatic negation ("He will not").
native_notes.121:5: The Hebrew root shamar ("guard, keep") recurs six times in verses 3-8 (as Qal participles in verses 3-5 and Qal imperfects in verses 7-8), unifying the psalm around the LORD's constant protection.
native_notes.122:3: The Pual verb chubberah-lah yachdav means literally "has been joined to itself together," depicting Jerusalem as a compact, tightly unified city.
native_notes.122:4: Hebrew uses the shortened poetic divine name Yah ("the LORD") in "tribes of the LORD"; edut ("decree," or "testimony") refers to the covenant stipulation requiring Israel's pilgrimage festivals.
native_notes.122:6: The Hebrew creates a sound play linking Yerushalayim ("Jerusalem"), shalom ("peace"), the Qal verb yishlayu ("may they be at ease"), and its cognate noun shalvah ("tranquility") in verse 7; the imperative sha'alu literally means "ask for" (that is, pray for).
native_notes.122:8: The Piel cohortative adabberah-na shalom bakh ("let me now speak peace within you") uses the Hebrew idiom "speak peace" (parallel to "seek good for you" in verse 9), though it may also be read as direct speech, "let me now say, 'Peace be within you.'"
native_notes.123:1: The form hayyoshvi ("who are seated") is the Qal active participle of yashav ("sit, dwell") with an archaic poetic connecting vowel -i (hireq compaginis), not a first-person suffix.
native_notes.123:2: Adonehem is morphologically plural ("their masters" or honorific plural "their master"), paired here with singular yad ("hand") and parallel to singular "her mistress."
native_notes.123:4: The ketiv reads as a single word ("of the proud"), whereas the translated qere divides it into two words: construct plural adjective "proud" governing the Qal active participle of yanah ("oppressors"), meaning "of proud oppressors." The verb "is sated" also takes an ethical dative ("for itself") intensifying "our soul."
native_notes.124:3: Azay is an emphatic poetic form of az ("then") attested only in vv. 3-5 of this psalm. The phrase "when their wrath burned" translates the active Qal infinitive construct of charah ("burn, grow hot").
native_notes.124:4: Nachlah appends an archaic poetic -ah ending to the masculine noun nachal ("torrent, wadi"), as confirmed by the masculine singular verb avar ("passed"). In drowning imagery, "our soul" (nephesh) can also evoke the throat or life itself.
native_notes.124:5: Hazzeydonim ("the seething") is a hapax legomenon from the root zid ("boil up, seethe; act insolently"), depicting turbulent, surging waters.
native_notes.125:2: "Jerusalem" stands as a fronted topic (casus pendens), and the Hebrew pairs the mountains around Jerusalem with the LORD around His people using simple "and" rather than an explicit comparative "as ... so."
native_notes.125:3: "Allotted portion" translates goral (literally "lot"), referring by metonymy to the inheritance allotted to the righteous. "Injustice" translates avlatah, appending an archaic poetic -ah ending to avlah.
native_notes.125:5: "Those who turn aside" is the Hiphil participle of natah used intransitively with "their crooked paths" as an adverbial accusative of direction. The particle et before "those who work iniquity" is the preposition "with" rather than a direct object marker, since the Hiphil verb yolikhem ("will lead them away") already carries the object suffix "them."
native_notes.126:1: The noun shivat ("fortunes/restoration") is a hapax legomenon from the root shuv ("return, turn back"), parallel to the idiom shuv shevut/shevit ("restore fortunes" or "bring back captivity").
native_notes.126:4: The Qere (read form) is shevitenu and the Ketiv (written form) is shevutenu; both belong to the Hebrew idiom shuv shevut/shevit ("restore fortunes" or "turn back captivity"). The noun afiqim refers to watercourses or seasonal streambeds in the arid Negev that fill rapidly after rain.
native_notes.126:6: The phrase meshekh-hazzara ("bag of seed") literally denotes a "drawing" or "pouch" of seed (often linked to the leather pouch carried while sowing, or to the trail of scattered seed; cf. Amos 9:13). Both clauses use the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction (halokh yelekh uvakho and bo-yavo) to convey continuous weeping while walking and certainty of coming in with joy.
native_notes.127:1: The Hebrew preposition le- in lishlomoh ("of Solomon") can indicate authorship ("by Solomon") or dedication ("for/concerning Solomon"). Both "a house" (bayit) and "a city" (ir) are indefinite in Hebrew, and the root shamar ("guard") is repeated in the participle shomer ("a guard").
native_notes.127:2: The final clause (ken yitten lidido shena) is a well-known Hebrew crux: shena ("sleep," spelled with an Aramaizing final aleph) is taken here as the direct object ("He gives sleep to His beloved"), though some read it adverbially ("so He provides for His beloved while sleeping"). The particle ken ("so/surely") is retained from the Masoretic Text rather than emended to ki ("for").
native_notes.127:5: The verbs "will not be put to shame" (yevoshu) and "speak" (yedabberu, Piel of dabar) shift to the plural in Hebrew, encompassing the father together with his sons (or such households generally) in legal or civic disputes at the city gate. Some scholars compare a homonymous root dabar ("drive back/subdue"), though "speak with" is the standard sense of Piel dabar with the preposition et.
native_notes.128:1: The wisdom exclamation ashrei ("how happy," also in 126:5 and 127:2) describes a flourishing state of well-being and is distinguished here from the verb barakh ("bless," Pual in v. 4 and Piel in v. 5).
native_notes.128:2: The phrase "the labor of your hands" (yegia kappekha, lit. "toil of your palms") is Hebrew metonymy for the yield produced by one's work. The conjunction ki following the fronted object is rendered emphatically ("indeed"), though it can also be taken temporally ("when").
native_notes.128:3: The noun yarketei ("inner parts") denotes the private interior quarters of the house, and shetilei ("saplings," a hapax legomenon from shatal, "to plant/transplant") refers to vigorous young olive shoots.
native_notes.129:3: The qere reads the singular lemaanitam ("their furrow"), whereas the ketiv reads the plural ("their furrows"); the preposition le- marks the direct object of the Hiphil verb heerikhu ("they lengthened").
native_notes.129:6: The Qal verb shalaph normally means "draw out" or "pull up"; here with the rare conjunction qadmat ("before") it is taken either intransitively ("before it shoots up") or with an indefinite subject ("before one pulls it up").
native_notes.129:7: The noun chitsno ("his arms") literally denotes the bosom or fold of a garment where cut stalks are cradled, and meammer ("sheaf-gatherer") is a Piel participle occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible.
native_notes.130:3: The divine name here is the shortened poetic form Yah (rendered "LORD"), paired with Adonai ("Lord"); the Qal verb shamar ("keep, watch") here carries the sense "keep account of."
native_notes.130:6: The opening clause is verbless in Hebrew, literally "My soul for the Lord," carrying forward the verb "waits" from verse 5; shomerim ("those keeping watch") is the Qal active participle of the same root shamar used in verse 3.
native_notes.130:7: The noun chesed denotes covenantal loyal love or steadfast faithfulness, and harbeh (the Hiphil infinitive absolute of rabah) functions adjectivally as "abundant."
native_notes.131:1: The verb hillakhti is the Piel stem of halakh ("walk"), expressing habitual conduct or going about, and niphlaot is the Niphal participle of pala ("be extraordinary" or "beyond comprehension").
native_notes.131:2: The opening im-lo (literally "if not") is an emphatic oath formula asserting what follows; shivviti (Piel of shavah, "level, calm") and domamti (Polel of damam, "still, silence") depict quieting inner restlessness, while alay (literally "upon me") is a Hebrew idiom for "within me" echoing aley immo ("upon his mother").
native_notes.132:1: The Hebrew form translated "his affliction" is a Pual infinitive construct from the root meaning "to be humbled" or "to be afflicted," literally "his being afflicted" or "all the hardship he endured."
native_notes.132:3: Hebrew introduces the clauses of verses 3-4 with the conditional particle "if," an elliptical oath idiom functioning as an emphatic negative ("I will certainly not...").
native_notes.132:6: The feminine singular suffix "it" refers to the ark (or the report of it), and "the fields of the forest" is a literal rendering of a phrase that likely alludes to Kiriath-jearim ("City of Forests"), where the ark rested (1 Sam 7:1-2), and can also be read as "the fields of Jaar."
native_notes.132:12: Hebrew uses the poetic relative pronoun "that" (zo) following the singular noun "My testimony" (written defectively without vav).
native_notes.132:18: The Qal verb translated "will gleam" (from the root tsits) can mean either "shine/gleam" (cf. the golden plate of Exod 28:36) or "blossom/flourish," echoing the image of "sprout" in verse 17.
native_notes.133:1: The Hebrew phrase translated "together as one" literally reads "even together" (gam-yachad), an emphatic adverbial expression for living in complete unity.
native_notes.133:2: Hebrew literally reads "the good oil" (echoing "good" in verse 1), denoting choice fragrant anointing oil, and "the collar of his garments" literally means "the mouth (neck-opening) of his garments" (cf. Exod 28:32). The participle "that descends" repeats the same verb used earlier in the verse and again in verse 3, and may modify either the oil or Aaron's beard.
native_notes.134:2: The noun "holy place" (qodesh) stands without a preposition as an adverbial accusative, meaning either directionally "toward the sanctuary" (cf. Ps 28:2) or adverbially "in holiness."
native_notes.134:3: Hebrew shifts from the plural commands of verses 1-2 to a singular object pronoun ("bless you"), reflecting a blessing pronounced upon the individual worshiper or Israel collectively.
native_notes.135:1: Hebrew uses the shortened divine name Yah in the opening "Praise the LORD" (halelu yah, literally "Hallelujah") as well as in verses 3, 4, and 21.
native_notes.135:3: The verb zammeru is a Piel imperative of zamar ("make music" or "sing praise"), and the adjective na'im ("delightful" or "pleasant") has no expressed subject, allowing either "it" (His name, or praising Him) or "He."
native_notes.135:14: In this covenantal context, yadin (Qal imperfect of din, "judge") carries the sense of deciding in favor of or vindicating His people, and yitnecham (Hithpael imperfect of nacham) expresses being moved to compassion or relenting.
native_notes.135:17: The verb ya'azinu (Hiphil imperfect of 'azan, derived from 'ozen, "ear") creates a wordplay with "ears" ("listen"), and the unusual double particle 'en-yesh emphasizes the complete absence of breath ("no breath at all").
native_notes.136:1: The refrain ki le'olam chasdo is a verbless Hebrew clause literally reading "for forever is His chesed," where chesed denotes loyal, covenantal love.
native_notes.136:13: Hebrew legozer ... ligzarim uses a cognate verb-and-noun phrase ("to the One who cuts into cut parts"), and yam-suph literally means "Sea of Reeds"; the Septuagint calls it the Red Sea.
native_notes.136:15: Hebrew ni'er (Piel perfect of na'ar) literally means "shook off" or "shook out," echoing Exodus 14:27.
native_notes.136:24: Hebrew wayyifreqenu (Qal wayyiqtol of paraq) literally means "tore us away" or "pulled us free," a verb used in late Biblical Hebrew and Aramaic for rescuing or delivering.
native_notes.137:2: Hebrew 'aravim refers to Euphrates poplars, and kinnorot specifically denotes stringed lyres.
native_notes.137:3: The noun tolalenu ("our tormentors") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; scholars debate whether it derives from yalal ("those who make us wail") or shalal ("our plunderers").
native_notes.137:5: The Masoretic text reads tishkach (Qal imperfect or jussive of shachach, "forget") with no stated object, repeating the verb from the first clause and implying that the musician's right hand would forget its skill.
native_notes.137:8: Hebrew hashshdudah (Qal passive participle of shadad, "devastate") literally means "the devastated one," used proleptically of Babylon's assured ruin.
native_notes.138:1: The Hebrew 'elohim' here denotes 'the gods' (or heavenly beings; some take it as human judges or rulers). Unlike the Septuagint, the Masoretic text does not include the divine name 'LORD' in this verse.
native_notes.138:2: Masoretic accentuation treats 'above all Your name' as a single prepositional phrase and 'Your word' as the direct object of the Hiphil verb 'higdalta' ('You have made great'), with no conjunction linking 'name' and 'word.'
native_notes.138:6: The form 'yeyeda' is an unusual Masoretic spelling and pointing of the Qal imperfect of 'yada' ('know') with a double yod.
native_notes.138:8: The idiom 'yigmor ba'adi' literally means 'will complete on my behalf,' with no explicit object expressed; 'ma'asei yadekha' ('the works of Your hands') is plural in the Masoretic text.
native_notes.139:3: The Piel verb 'zerita' (from z-r-h, 'winnow' or 'sift,' or a homonym meaning 'measure out') is used metaphorically for close scrutiny of the psalmist's movement and rest.
native_notes.139:6: Translates the Qere 'peli'ah' ('too marvelous/wonderful'); the Ketiv 'pl'yh' represents an alternate feminine adjective formation with the same meaning.
native_notes.139:11: The rare Qal verb 'yeshufeni' (from sh-w-f) means 'bruise' or 'crush' in Genesis 3:15 and Job 9:17, and here conveys darkness overwhelming or engulfing the speaker.
native_notes.139:16: Translates the Qere 'we-lo' ('and to Him [belongs] one among them,' or 'for it' referring to 'my unformed substance'); the Ketiv reads 'we-lo'' ('and not'), yielding 'when there was not yet one of them.' The noun 'golem' ('unformed substance') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible.
native_notes.139:20: The Masoretic wording is terse: 'yomrukha' is a shortened Qal form of 'yo'mrukha' ('speak of You'), 'nasu'' reflects Qal perfect 'nas'u' ('take up,' with 'Your name' implied from the idiom of Exodus 20:7), and 'arekha' means 'Your adversaries' (cf. 1 Samuel 28:16).
native_notes.140:8: The Masoretic text reverses the usual 'Lord GOD' sequence, placing the divine name before Adonai and pointing the divine name with the vowels of 'Elohim' ('GOD, the Lord').
native_notes.140:10: Translates the Qere 'yekhasemo' (3ms Piel imperfect of k-s-h, agreeing with singular 'amal,' 'trouble/mischief'); the Ketiv reads a 3mp verb 'ykswmw' ('may they cover them').
native_notes.140:11: Translates the Qere 'yimmotu' (Niphal imperfect of m-w-t, 'fall'); the Ketiv reads Hiphil 'ymytw' ('let them cause to fall'). The following Hiphil 'yappilem' ('may He cast them') is active 3ms, and 'mahamorot' ('deep pits') is a hapax legomenon.
native_notes.140:12: The major poetic accent (oleh we-yored) divides the verse at 'in the land,' placing 'man of violence' and 'evil' in the second half; 'le-madhefot' (from d-h-f, 'thrust/drive headlong') is a hapax legomenon denoting repeated blows or headlong ruin.
native_notes.140:13: Translates the Qere 'yada'ti' (Qal perfect 1cs, 'I know'); the Ketiv 'yd't' is a defective spelling of the same 1cs form (or 2ms, 'You know').
native_notes.141:3: The verb nitsrah is an unusual vocalization of the Qal imperative masculine singular (with paragogic heh and dagesh forte in the second radical) of natsar ("keep watch"), and dal is a rare poetic masculine form corresponding to delet ("door").
native_notes.141:5: In this famously terse Masoretic verse, shemen rosh can mean either "oil for the head" or "finest oil" (playing on roshi, "my head"), and yani is a defective Hiphil jussive of nu ("refuse, reject"). The final clause literally reads "for still, even my prayer is against [or amid] their evil deeds."
native_notes.141:6: The phrase bidey-sela literally means "by the hands of a crag," a Hebrew idiom for the sides of a cliff. The Niphal perfect nishmetu ("cast down") with the following weqatal may be rendered with future/prophetic or past/gnomic force.
native_notes.141:8: The Masoretic text reverses the usual divine title, placing the divine name before Adonai (the divine name pointed as Elohim: "GOD, the Lord"). The apocopated Piel jussive tear from arah literally means "pour out" or "empty out," conveying leaving one's life defenseless to death.
native_notes.141:10: The noun phrase literally reads "into his nets," a distributive singular referring to each of the wicked. Following the Masoretic atnach after resha'im ("the wicked"), yachad ("together, at the same time") opens the second clause alongside the emphatic pronoun anokhi ("I myself").
native_notes.142:1: "Maskil" transliterates a technical psalm superscription of uncertain exact sense, connected to the root sakal ("have insight" or "act skillfully").
native_notes.142:5: Habbit is a Hiphil infinitive absolute of nabat ("look") functioning imperatively alongside the Qal imperative ure'eh ("and see").
native_notes.142:8: Masger ("confinement, prison") derives from sagar ("shut in"). The Hiphil imperfect yakhtiru ("will encircle") from katar means "surround me," or possibly "crown themselves on my account."
native_notes.143:6: The second clause is verbless in Hebrew ("my soul is like a parched land for You"), leaving the implied thirsting or longing unstated.
native_notes.143:9: Eleykha khissiti uses the Piel perfect of kasah ("cover, conceal") without an explicit object—literally "to You I have covered [myself]," meaning hidden myself or taken cover with You, whereas the Septuagint implies a different verb ("I have fled").
native_notes.143:10: Tovah ("good") lacks the definite article and bears the Masoretic atnach, and the Hiphil imperfect tancheni ("guide me") from nachah can be parsed as either third-person feminine singular ("may Your good Spirit guide me") or second-person masculine singular ("Your Spirit is good; guide me").
native_notes.144:2: The MT reads עַמִּי ("my people"); several Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions (LXX, Syriac, Targum) read עַמִּים ("peoples"). The noun חַסְדִּי ("my loyal love") is applied directly to God as a personal epithet.
native_notes.144:6: The Qal imperative בְּרוֹק ("flash") is the sole verbal occurrence of the root ברק in the Hebrew Bible, paired here with its cognate noun בָּרָק ("lightning").
native_notes.144:12: The particle אֲשֶׁר functions here as a purpose or result conjunction ("so that"), linking the petition for deliverance in v. 11 to the blessings of vv. 12-14. Both מְגֻדָּלִים ("grown large") and מְחֻטָּבוֹת ("carved") are Pual participles.
native_notes.144:14: The Pual participle מְסֻבָּלִים ("heavily laden," from סבל) with אַלּוּפֵינוּ ("our cattle") and the clauses "no breach and no going out" can refer either to city security (no breached wall or exile) or to livestock fertility (cattle heavy with young, suffering no miscarriage or loss).
native_notes.145:6: Ketiv/Qere: the written text (ketiv) has plural וגדלותיך ("Your great deeds"), while the read text (qere) translated here has singular וּגְדֻלָּתְךָ ("Your greatness"), agreeing with the 3fs resumptive suffix on the Piel verb אֲסַפְּרֶנָּה ("I will recount it").
