native_notes.145:12: The MT shifts from 2nd-person suffixes in v. 11 to 3rd-person suffixes here (גְּבוּרֹתָיו, "His mighty deeds"; מַלְכוּתוֹ, "His kingdom"); some ancient versions harmonize both to 2nd person ("Your").
native_notes.145:13: This psalm is an alphabetical acrostic in Hebrew; the MT moves directly from the Mem verse (v. 13) to the Samekh verse (v. 14) with no Nun verse (a Nun verse appears in 11QPsa, LXX, and Syriac).
native_notes.145:16: The noun רָצוֹן ("desire," cf. v. 19) can also denote God's "favor" or "goodwill," allowing the alternate sense "satisfying every living creature with favor."
native_notes.146:4: The wordplay between בֶּן־אָדָם ("a human being," v. 3) and אֲדָמָה ("ground," v. 4) recalls humanity's return to the soil. The noun עֶשְׁתֹּנֹתָיו ("his plans") is a biblical hapax legomenon of Aramaic origin.
native_notes.146:8: Literally "opens the blind"; the Qal verb פקח is used specifically of opening eyes (and rarely ears), so English supplies "the eyes of."
native_notes.146:9: The rare Polel imperfect יְעוֹדֵד ("He sustains," from עוד) contrasts with the Piel imperfect יְעַוֵּת ("He subverts," from עות, literally "make crooked").
native_notes.147:1: The form rendered "to make music" is a Piel infinitive construct with a feminine ending taking "our God" as its direct object and serving as the subject of "good." The masculine adjective "pleasant" either refers impersonally to making music ("it is pleasant") or describes God ("He is pleasant").
native_notes.147:5: Literally "to His understanding there is no number," intentionally echoing "number" in 146:4 to contrast the countable stars with God's uncountable understanding.
native_notes.147:7: The Qal imperative "Respond" comes from the Hebrew root meaning "answer" or "respond," used in liturgical contexts for responsive singing and praise.
native_notes.147:14: "The choicest wheat" translates a Hebrew idiom literally meaning "fat of wheat," where "fat" denotes the richest or finest portion.
native_notes.147:19: The consonants are written defectively without a yod (ketiv singular, "His word"), whereas the Masoretic vocalization reads the qere plural ("His words"), matching the plural "decrees" and "rulings" that follow.
native_notes.147:20: The Masoretic Hebrew text reads literally "and as for rulings, they have not known them" without a possessive suffix ("His"), unlike the Septuagint.
native_notes.148:2: As in 147:8, the consonants are written without a yod (ketiv singular, "His host"), while the vocalization reads the qere plural ("His hosts" or "His armies"), denoting God's heavenly forces.
native_notes.148:6: The masculine singular imperfect verb "will not pass away" takes "decree" as its subject; alternatively, it may be understood impersonally or distributively as "which none may transgress."
native_notes.148:8: The noun rendered "fog" literally denotes thick rising smoke or vapor and here refers to dense mist or fog alongside snow.
native_notes.148:14: "Horn" is a common Hebrew idiom for strength, dignity, or victory. The final phrase is literally "a people of His near one," a poetic expression for a people close to God.
native_notes.149:1: Hebrew halelu-yah ("Hallelujah"), a Piel imperative of halal ("praise") with Yah, the shortened poetic form of the divine name, recurs in 149:9, 150:1, and 150:6. "Devoted ones" translates chasidim, denoting those bound to God in covenant loyalty (chesed).
native_notes.149:2: Hebrew be'osav uses a masculine plural Qal active participle of 'asah ("make") with a singular suffix, literally "in its Makers," an idiom known as the plural of majesty referring to God (cf. Job 35:10; Isa 54:5).
native_notes.149:6: Hebrew cherev pifiyyot is literally "a sword of edges" (from a reduplicated plural of peh, "mouth" or "edge"). Both "throat" and "hand" are singular in Hebrew with plural suffixes, used distributively for each worshiper.
native_notes.149:9: Hebrew mishpat katuv ("written judgment," using the Qal passive participle of katav) refers to a recorded divine decree; hadar ("honor") carries the nuance of royal splendor or distinction.
native_notes.150:1: Hebrew beqodsho can mean spatially "in His holy place" (sanctuary), matching the spatial parallel "in the expanse of His strength" (the heavenly vault, raqia'), or abstractly "in His holiness."
native_notes.150:3: Hebrew teqa' (occurring only here, from taqa', "blow") denotes a loud blast of the shofar (curved animal horn). The nevel was a larger plucked stringed instrument (rendered "lute" here) paired here with the kinnor ("lyre").
native_notes.150:5: Literally "cymbals of sound" (shama') and "cymbals of shouting" (teru'ah), likely distinguishing clearer, resonant cymbals from louder, clashing cymbals.
native_notes.150:6: Hebrew kol haneshamah is literally "all the breath," a collective idiom for every breathing creature, construed with the feminine singular Piel jussive tehallel ("may [it] praise").
